04-732.name: User Experience Design
04-732.desc: With over 1 billion websites and 3 million mobile apps worldwide, creating applications that enhance user satisfaction and engagement is crucial for success. This course introduces students to the core principles of user experience (UX), from identifying user needs through research to developing and evaluating low- and high-fidelity prototypes using heuristics, formal evaluations, and usability testing. In the second half of the course, students will study how people see, hear, and think, and evidence-based principles for building usable and visually appealing interfaces. The course features lectures and individual and group design tasks, culminating in a group project that integrates user research, iterative prototyping, and user testing.

67-282.name: Special Topics: AI and Data Science for Intelligent Healthcare Systems
67-282.desc: This course introduces students to the application of artificial intelligence and data science in healthcare, with a focus on multimodal systems that integrate clinical, textual, and sensor data. Students will learn key techniques in machine learning, natural language processing, and data integration to develop and evaluate models for healthcare prediction, monitoring, and decision support. The course emphasizes applied understanding of how AI-driven approaches can advance intelligent and data-enabled healthcare systems.

95-762.name: Decision Modeling
95-762.desc: This course is for Heinz students in the AIM degree program.  This course is one of several Heinz College courses in analytics and management science that survey a variety of hands-on quantitative modeling methods that are useful for making better evidence-based decisions. They are tailored for particular programs but overlap considerably, so students cannot take courses from more than one of these sequences because they overlap so much.  This course covers multicriteria decision making (MCDM), optimization, Monte Carlo simulation, risk-return tradeoffs, decision analysis, and forecasting. Considerable emphasis is placed on understanding the strengths and limitations of each method and so when to use which. Relative to other parallel courses, more time is spent discussing how to integrate multiple objectives or attributes, both quantifiable and non-quantifiable.

95-864.name: AI Model Development
95-864.desc: This is a core class for AIM students and they will receive priority for enrollment. If seats remain after AIM students are registered, those on the waitlist will be invited.  Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping how we reason, generate structured outputs, and build intelligent systems. At the core of these capabilities are transformer-based architectures and scalable pipelines for adapting, evaluating, and deploying models in production. AI Model Development is a rigorous, hands-on course that teaches students how to design, refine, and operationalize LLM-based systems across diverse real-world applications.  The course opens with a focused review of ML/DL foundations and transitions rapidly into LLM fundamentals—tokenization, embeddings, attention, and decoding. Students learn to engineer prompts, construct retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, adapt models using fine-tuning and parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, QLoRA), and evaluate safety, alignment, and performance with tools like MMLU, GSM8K, and pass@k.  In later modules, students develop agentic workflows by integrating tools, memory, and reasoning into LLM systems. Domain-specific applications are explored in software engineering and biosciences, including protein design with AlphaFold and AlphaEvolve. As one student noted, "NLX/LLM is quite useful as its contents are closely related to the latest trends of AI and the job requirements of most AI/ML engineer positions."

95-897.name: Machine Learning Technologies
95-897.desc: This course offers a foundational introduction to the principles, methodologies, and applications of modern machine learning (ML); from foundational principles to cutting-edge methods across diverse data modalities. It is organized into three broad parts. Part I focuses on the foundations of supervised learning, emphasizing classical models such as linear and logistic regression, decision trees, and ensemble methods. The goal is to equip students with the understanding of the ML workflow, model evaluation, and generalization principles. Core concepts such as bias-variance tradeoff, interpretability, uncertainty, robustness, and fairness are introduced early, preparing students to think critically about model performance and reliability. This part also introduces the contemporary learning paradigms including self-supervised, semi-supervised, active, meta, continual, reinforcement, and federated learning to showcase the diverse settings under which ML is developed.  Building on this foundation, Part II introduces modern models including neural networks and advanced architectures such as convolutional, recurrent, and attention-based models. Finally, Part III focuses on ML techniques for specialized data modalities—tabular, graph, temporal, text, and image data—and their practical applications such as forecasting, recommendation, fraud detection.  By the end of the course, students will have a comprehensive understanding of both the theoretical underpinnings and the practical considerations involved in designing and applying machine learning techniques.

49-205.name: Tech Venture Marketing for Engineers
49-205.desc: Designed for engineers, this course will cover key strategic and tactical marketing concepts and methods: product adoption life cycle, customer segmentation, strategic market planning and tactical considerations, with special considerations for new high-tech engineering products and innovations. This course will equip technologists with a marketing perspective, equipping them to achieve market adoption and sales growth.

49-406.name: Tech Venture Formation
49-406.desc: The course will cover key aspects for venture formation: intellectual property; deal structures, term sheets and contracts; venture financing and financial statements. Although presented in the context of technology startups, these frameworks and methodologies are useful for corporate new-business-development and new-market-entry as well.

49-767.name: Organizational Behavior for High Tech Knowledge Industry
49-767.desc: This course is about "organizational behavior" for high tech knowledge workers. Organizations are essentially human institutions. They are created by people, populated by people, managed by people, developed by people and operated by people. Understanding the fundamentals of human behavior is crucial for success. But people need to be grouped together and "organized" in order to make things happen, often under tight time and budgetary constraints. This course will focus on high tech organizational design and team effectivenessin other words, on the "execution" capability of a knowledge enterprise. Specifically, we will discuss how to organize a team, a business unit, or a company (including start-ups) that are operating in dynamic, global high tech ecosystems.   The focus is on agility, flexibility, and the capacity to adapt to new business realities or crisis situations. High tech companies need innovative capabilities, entrepreneurial approaches, cross-silo collaboration, and resilient dispositions. A major challenge is to devise collaborative teams & organizational structures capable of making "sudden turns" and accommodating changing realities.

11-766.name: Large Language Model Applications
11-766.desc: Large language models are used today for many more applications than just modelling language. In this course, we learn how Transformer-based neural language models have been adapted for applications ranging from web agents and retrieval systems to music generation and coding and writing assistants. We will systematically examine the ways different applications adapt the base technologies underlying large language models through varying choices in pre-training and fine-tuning data, model architecture, training objective, and usage of inference-time compute. This class is intended for students who have already learned the basics of how language models are implemented and are curious to develop an understanding of the advanced techniques used for customizing them to different applications.

11-787.name: AI Cofounder: A Startup Builder's Guide
11-787.desc: AI Cofounder: A Startup Builder's Guide is a 13-week, project-based course for students who want to launch AI-centered startups and lead as the technical or AI cofounder. The course offers a practical framework for ideating, building, leading, and scaling a technology venture—from idea to market validation and fundraising prep—while adapting in real time to evolving AI tools and trends. Through applied workshops, founder stories, and domain-specific case studies (fintech, health-tech, climate, and more), students will develop their own founder's playbook, translating technical expertise into entrepreneurial action. By the end of the course, each participant will have crafted a validated startup concept with a financial plan, go-to-market strategy, and pitch, culminating in a public poster session during AIVS.co's demo day.

11-977.name: Multi Modal Machine Learning
11-977.desc: Multimodal machine learning (MMML) is a vibrant multi-disciplinary research field which addresses some of the original goals of artificial intelligence by integrating and modeling multiple communicative modalities, including linguistic, acoustic and visual messages. With the initial research on audio-visual speech recognition and more recently with language vision projects such as image and video captioning, this research field brings some unique challenges for multimodal researchers given the heterogeneity of the data and the contingency often found between modalities.  The course will present the fundamental mathematical concepts in machine learning and deep learning relevant to the five main challenges in multimodal machine learning: (1) multimodal representation learning, (2) translation & mapping, (3) modality alignment, (4) multimodal fusion and (5) co-learning.  These include, but not limited to, multimodal auto-encoder, deep canonical correlation analysis, multi-kernel learning, attention models and multimodal recurrent neural networks. We will also review recent papers describing state-of-the-art probabilistic models and computational algorithms for MMML and discuss the current and upcoming challenges. The course will discuss many of the recent applications of MMML including multimodal affect recognition, image and video captioning and cross-modal multimedia retrieval. This is a remote offering only available to certificate seeking students.

82-060.name: Arab Society in Flux: Migration, Displacement, and Cultural Change

82-061.name: Chinese Art: Calligraphy and Painting
82-061.desc: The course aims at providing students with basic knowledge of Chinese calligraphy and painting, and how it mirrors Chinese history, culture and philosophy. Key topics include the introduction of Chinese writing system, its cultural content, and the skills in calligraphy and painting. Combined with experiential learning and hands-on practice, the course will give students the tools, not only appreciate the masterpieces in museum collections, but also talk about Chinese art in social, business and academic settings. Some of the topics we will study include the concepts of calligraphy styles, landscape painting and the status of the artists in dynasties. No prerequisites required, no previous art experience is expected, and open to students from all disciplines.

82-175.name: Elementary Japanese 1 Online
82-175.desc: Whether you are learning Japanese for the first time or reconnecting with a language tied to your heritage or personal interests, this course supports your development as a language user and finding your new identities in speaking Japanese. Throughout the semester, you will build foundational skills in listening, speaking, reading, and writing Japanese while exploring how language reflects and shapes identity and community membership. Through everyday contexts—such as making plans, visiting someone's home, or participating in classroom life—you will consider questions like: What makes a request polite in Japanese? How do we express who we are in a new language? How does a community shape communication and connection? This online course combines weekly in-person practice with flexible, self-paced online work using an interactive eBook designed for independent and collaborative learning. Students are encouraged to bring curiosity, questions, and personal experiences into our shared learning space.

82-188.name: Global Science Fiction
82-188.desc: This innovative, team-taught course introduces students to Science Fiction as a global mode of storytelling that reflects and reimagines human experiences across diverse cultural, historical, and political contexts. Through comparative case studies from The Americas, Asia, and Europe, students will explore how different societies use speculative fiction to question colonial legacies, technological transformations, conceptions of human body and intelligence, environmental crises, and visions of the future.  By examining science fiction through literature, film, comics, and media, the course situates the genre within its local and transnational frameworks—highlighting how histories of empire, migration, and modernization shape global imaginaries of progress, identity, and survival. Students will engage with key debates in cultural and literary studies while developing tools to interpret science fiction as a critical lens on real-world challenges, from artificial intelligence and climate change to inequality and posthuman ethics.  Through active, collaborative learning, students will develop contextual thinking skills by analyzing how each work emerges from and responds to its specific cultural moment. By the end of the course, students will be able to identify how global science fiction both mirrors and critiques contemporary societies, and how their own ways of imagining the future are shaped by context.  Course taught in English. No prior knowledge of science fiction required.

82-254.name: Korean Media & Professional Communication: Building Career-Ready Language Skills
82-254.desc: Transform your love of Korean pop culture into professional language skills that open career doors. This intermediate course welcomes both heritage and non-heritage speakers who want to develop workplace-ready Korean while exploring contemporary media and digital culture. Using authentic materials from K-dramas, webtoons, social media, and business content, you'll build practical communication skills for professional settings. Whether you're interested in Korean companies, international business, content creation, translation, or cultural industries, this course provides the language foundation and cultural literacy you need. We'll progress from analyzing how professionals are portrayed in Korean media to developing your own professional communication skills. By semester's end, you'll have a portfolio of work samples, networking language, and the confidence to use Korean in professional contexts.

82-443.name: Spanish Reading and Translation Workshop
82-443.desc: This course is an advanced introduction to professional translation from Spanish to English and vice versa as a professional practice. The objective is for students to learn the theory and practice of translation while reviewing linguistic subfields such syntax (word order), semantics (meaning), lexicology (vocabulary), pragmatics (language use and context), and sociolinguistics (language in relation to social factors). Accurate translation also requires in-depth study of culture-broadly defined-and its role in localization. Students will work with moderately to highly difficult texts across a number of genres, e.g., non-specialized and specialized texts, those that combine words and images, and professional and literary texts. Students will increase their critical reading, research, and general localization skills, and develop proficiency in using AI for translation and evaluating and post-editing its resulting product.

10-202.name: Introduction to Modern AI
10-202.desc: This course provides an introduction to how modern AI systems work.  By "modern AI", we specifically mean the machine learning methods and large language models (LLMs) behind systems like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude. Despite their seemingly amazing generality, the basic techniques that underlie these AI models are surprisingly simple: a minimal LLM implementation leverages a fairly small set of machine learning methods and architectures, and can be written in a few hundred lines of code.    This course will guide you through the basic methods that will let you implement a basic AI chatbot.  You will learn the basics of supervised machine learning, large language models, and post-training.  By the end of the course you will be able to write the code that runs an open source LLM from scratch, as well as code train these models based upon a corpus of data.  The material we cover will include: a brief history of AI; supervised machine learning -- including linear models, loss functions and optimization, and neural networks; large language models -- including self attention and transformers, tokenizers, and efficient inference; and post-training -- including supervised fine tuning, alignment and instruction tuning, reasoning models and reinforcement learning, and safety and security of AI systems.

27-323.name: Powder Processing of Materials
27-323.desc: This course addresses the methods used in, and the principles that underlie, powder processing of metals and ceramics. Aspects of powder processing will be discussed in relation to the use of materials in engineering applications. The relationship between processing methods and materials performance in select applications will be discussed using specific materials examples including metals and ceramics. The course is broken down into three main parts: (1) understanding, selecting, and controlling powder characteristics; (2) powder handling, compaction, and forming techniques; and (3) drying, burnout, densification, sintering, and grain growth in powder compacts. Topics include chemical thermodynamics, reaction kinetics, surfaces, colloids, dispersions, process engineering, powder handling, powder compaction, shape forming, densification, and sintering.

27-618.name: SPECIAL TOPICS: Laboratory Techniques for Electrochemically Functional Materials
27-618.desc: This is a laboratory-based class focused on teaching the fundamentals of performing electrochemical characterization on functional materials,  along with making useful devices such as batteries, fuel cells, and electrolyzers. In the course of the class, students will both synthesize and characterize a range of materials, and the class will culminate in the completion of a device demonstration project

27-718.name: Soft Materials
27-718.desc: The emphasis in this course will be on the emerging unifying physical principles that explain the  macroscopic properties of a wide variety of soft materials, e.g., colloids, liquid crystals,  surfactants, polymers, and biological structures. At the end of the course, students should  understand the concepts, experimental techniques, and open questions in the field. The course is  interdisciplinary, and it is expected that enrollment will cover a wide spectrum of students.  Therefore, the essential concepts will be taught as necessary.    Prerequisites: Graduate standing or permission of instructor.

21-312.name: Topics in Applied Mathematics
21-312.desc: This course affords students with the opportunity to study topics which are in the area of expertise of the instructor.  This course may taken more than once if content is sufficiently different.  Course prerequisites will depend on the content of the course.  Please see the course URL for semester-specific topics.  (Three 50 minute lectures)

21-318.name: Topics in Pure Mathematics
21-318.desc: This course affords students with the opportunity to study topics which are in the area of expertise of the instructor.  This course may taken more than once if content is sufficiently different.  Course prerequisites will depend on the content of the course.  Please see the course URL for semester-specific topics.  (Three 50 minute lectures)

24-609.name: Special Topics: Entertainment Engineering
24-609.desc: Special Topics: Entertainment Engineering is a small group, collaborative problem solving class intended to bring together the skillsets of students in Drama Design & Production and Mechanical Engineering. The group will spend the semester coming up with a novel solution to a real world backstage problem provided by an outside entertainment production company. Mentoring will come from Engineering, Drama, and outside professionals. The project will involve ideation and problem solving, drawing and detailing, and shop prototyping. Some travel may be required. Participation by instructor permission only.

24-641.name: Special Topics: Application of AI and ML Methods for Modern Manufacturing
24-641.desc: Manufacturing, the art of making things, is of increasing importance to economic stability and national security. While mechanical components have been manufactured by machines since the dawn of Industrial Revolution, recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) promise to change this area beyond imagination.   Through a series of projects, this course will introduce the AI and ML tools affecting the modern manufacturing techniques. The course will begin with a comprehensive review of the available manufacturing processes from nano to macro length scales. A high-level overview of the AI and ML methods will then be provided including computer vision techniques, LLMs, generative design etc. Using this knowledge, student groups will develop: (i) an automated defect detection system by training images of manufactured goods via an online CNN-based platform, (ii) a low-code agentic AI framework for controlling manufacturing processes, (iii) an AI-based workflow development and fabrication of part using 5-axis machining center; and (iv) virtual robot programming for typical industrial automation processes. Students will thus gain practical experience by using popular AI/ML frameworks to solve real-world manufacturing problems. This course is designed to equip students with the necessary skills to innovate and lead in the future of intelligent manufacturing.  Students are expected to have an introductory background in AI / ML fundamentals (e.g., 24-787 or other equivalent course) and proficiency in basic Python programming.

24-660.name: Special Topics: Crafted Matter
24-660.desc: This class explores how we may understand handicrafts through the lens of mechanics. Historically, craft-based actions—such as folding, cutting, weaving, and molding—are commonly associated to their use generating complex forms for creative expression. From the engineer's perspective, these simple and iterative techniques are useful for embedding desirable properties into materials. We will survey this paradigm for building designer materials by studying the history, mechanical fundamentals, and state-of-the-art research for modeling and designing crafted matter. The course will include experiential practice of crafts as well as theoretic considerations with an eye towards application in emerging technologies. The handicrafts covered include:   I. Paper crafts (e.g., origami, kirigami);  II. Woven crafts (e.g., knits, beadwork, baskets); and  III. Forming crafts (e.g., glasswork, balloon art, pottery).  A sampling of the mechanics topics covered include: slender structures, viscous flows, topological mechanics. Students are expected to have strong undergraduate backgrounds in fluid and solid mechanics.  Assessment will be done following a "specifications grading" scheme. Standard assignments will include:   1. Pre-Class assignments covering readings and concepts that introduce ideas covered in lectures   2. In-class activities including participation in peer presentations, crafting workshops, and guest lecturers.  3. Problem sets covering core class content.  4. Projects including written and oral communications exploring advanced mechanics of a handicraft of your choosing.

24-880.name: AI Agents for Engineers
24-880.desc: This course provides engineers with the theoretical background and hands-on skills to design and deploy LLM-based agents that streamline and enhance engineering workflows. This course introduces students to the integration of models like GPT, Claude, Gemini, and LLaMA into engineering pipelines for simulation, optimization, analysis, and documentation in real-world applications. Students will learn about LLM internals, prompting, fine-tuning, and frameworks for building agents capable of reasoning, planning, and using tools across complex engineering tasks. The course centers on LLMs as autonomous collaborators that can interact with CAD tools, simulations, APIs, and codebases to perform tasks such as simulation setup, technical report generation, code development, and design optimization. Topics include retrieval-augmented generation, multi-agent systems, tool calling, agent memory, and human-in-the-loop workflows. Students will complete hands-on assignments and a capstone project applying LLM agents to a specific engineering domain such as robotics, materials, or biomedicine. By the end, students will be able to design, evaluate, and deploy reliable LLM agents in practical engineering settings.

57-443.name: Diverse Populations in Inclusive Settings
57-443.desc: Diverse Populations in Inclusive Settings is an introduction to issues in music education with and among a broad range of diverse student populations. Specific musical characteristics and needs of multiple types of learners will be examined, including: English Language Learners and students from varied backgrounds, racial and cultural origins, gender and sexual minorities, and urban/rural under-resourced learning contexts. There will be an emphasis on special needs in music education, including physical, intellectual, cognitive, emotional, and sensory challenges, and the learning process. Information and guidelines regarding state and federal regulatory issues related to special needs education will form the foundation for the topics included in this class. Field experience may be required. The course will explore the transformative impact of music education through a praxis lens and examine socio-inclusive issues in the music education classroom. Philosophical foundations are grounded in Paulo Freire's Pedagogy of the Oppressed, Estelle Jorgensen's Transforming Music Education and Markku Kaikkonen's philosophical manifesto in Music for All. Educational theory is derived from Susan Raponi's Learning Differentiation in Music Education Theory, foundations of which are grounded in Howard Gardner's Frames of Mind, David Elliott and Marissa Silverman's Music Matters, and Carol Tomlinson's How to Differentiate Instruction.

57-462.name: Vocal Pedagogy II
57-462.desc: This course serves to introduce students to the methodology aspect of vocal pedagogy, which requires a basic knowledge of anatomy, and general knowledge of vocal physiology.  We will be hold in-class demonstrations on the broader topics covered in Vocal Pedagogy I, including but not limited to registration, posture, breathing for singing, resonance, formant tuning and articulation.   In addition to classroom presentations, the professor will assign readings and give classroom lectures on working with students, assessing your strengths, and becoming critical thinkers.

57-573.name: Special Topics in Theory and Analysis
57-573.desc: Special topics courses in theory and analysis are developed to cover emerging issues or specialized content not represented in the existing music curriculum. These upper-level explorations of highly specialized subject matter and content vary from semester to semester. Students cannot repeat an individual section of a special topics course, but they can register for other sections. Undergraduate enrollment may be contingent upon instructor approval only.

57-577.name: Special Topics in Musicology and Music History
57-577.desc: Special topics courses in musicology and music history are developed to cover emerging issues or specialized content not represented in the existing music curriculum. These upper-level explorations of highly specialized subject matter and content vary from semester to semester. Students cannot repeat an individual section of a special topics course, but they can register for other sections.

57-628.name: Keyboard Studies for Graduate Music Education II
57-628.desc: Continues 57608 Keyboard Studies for Graduate Music Education I. This course develops piano skills necessary for work in the elementary and secondary schools. Special emphasis is placed on transposition, score reading, harmonization, and sight-reading.

57-668.name: Opera Studies Seminar
57-668.desc: The Opera Studies Seminar offers immersive and intensive historical and analytical study of specific topics in opera studies, including the works of particular composers, eras, or languages. Other topics/subjects may be offered depending upon the instructor. At its most basic, the course structure involves the intense study of performance texts and immersion in relevant primary and secondary material. As an upper-level seminar, this course also has heavy reading and writing expectations. Topic for Fall 2026: The Operas of Benjamin Britten

57-742.name: Sonatas/Songs for Collaborative Pianists II
57-742.desc: Continues 57741. This course will be focused on Collaborative Piano performances and students' presentations on specific subjects related to the performance of collaborative piano works, both instrumental and vocal. During the semester students will have the experience of playing live performances, as well as listening and commenting on other students' performances. Other special projects will be assigned as needed.

57-836.name: English/Contemporary Vocal Literature and Repertoire
57-836.desc: The course provides a bibliography of vocal repertoire in the English language. Material will be limited to art songs and will be presented via individual student or group performances in class and recorded performances. Research assignments will be required for selected anthologies or for works by specific composers. Repertoire will be examined according to vocal requirements, musical style, and programmatic function. The repertoire will consist primarily of works by British and American composers, but works by Russian and Spanish composers will also be included.

57-840.name: Sprezzatura: Career Skills in Language IV
57-840.desc: Conclusion of the four-semester Sprezzatura sequence for graduate Collaborative Piano students.

57-852.name: English Diction
57-852.desc: The aim of the course is to bring students into a deeper and broader experience of English Diction. This one-semester course helps singers sing English songs from the Classical and Musical Theater repertoire with clarity, accuracy, ease, uniformity, and expressiveness; to illuminate meaning; and to improve tonal quality through diction.

57-877.name: Special Topics in Musicology and Music History
57-877.desc: Special topics courses in musicology and music history are developed to cover emerging issues or specialized content not represented in the existing music curriculum. These upper-level explorations of highly specialized subject matter and content vary from semester to semester. Students cannot repeat an individual section of a special topics course, but they can register for other sections.

80-260.name: Dangerous Ideas in Psychiatry
80-260.desc: One day in 19th century France a young man abandons his workplace at a local gas company, wanders off into one general direction without saying goodbye to his loved ones, and winds up on a different continent with little memory of his travels. Soon others follow, not to the same destination but scattered to various foreign lands and cities, enough to cause a short-lived epidemic of compelled vagrancy that would spread from France to Italy, Germany, and Russia before wearing off and leaving the clinical textbooks again. What could it mean for a mental illness to be "real" if it only exists for a time and place? Can things like a particular immigration policy or the popularization of the bicycle contribute to the explanation or even the cause of a diagnosed medical condition? And do people in different societies experience a serious condition like schizophrenia differently? In this class we will study cases in psychiatry that are both politically and scientifically controversial. We will look primarily at culture-bound syndromes which can be specific to certain societies, demographics, countries, and even certain times in history. The class will be centered around individual student projects. You will get to choose a relevant medical phenomenon and explore it from scientific, philosophical, and historical angles throughout the course of the class. I will provide a pool of suitable topics for you to pick from. You are most welcome to suggest a relevant topic that you found yourself. There will be no exams. Instead, there will be a steady and moderate workload in the form of weekly and biweekly assignments pertaining to our readings and your projects so you can receive continuous feedback on how well you apply the general concepts of this class to the individual cases you chose.

80-714.name: Logics for Knowledge and Belief
80-714.desc: Standard logical languages can express negation ("not p"), conjunction ("p and q"), material implication ("if p then q"), quantification ("for all x, p(x)"), etc. But they don't directly capture statements like the following:  "Alice knows p." "Henceforth, it will be the case that p." "It ought to be the case that p." "If it had been the case that p, it would have been the case that q." "Everybody knows p." "Everybody knows that everybody knows p." "Infinitely often in the future, p will be true." "After an announcement of p, it will be the case that Alice knows q." "If p is not permitted, then you ought to know that p is not permitted." etc. Modal logic is a very general framework for systematically reasoning about statements like these. This course is an introduction to mathematical modal logic and its applications in philosophy, computer science, linguistics, and economics, with emphasis on epistemic interpretations (i.e., logics for representing and reasoning about knowledge/belief). We begin with a rigorous development of propositional modal logic: the basic language, interpretation in relational structures, axiom systems, proofs, and validity. We prove soundness and completeness of various systems using the canonical model method and study model equivalence and expressivity results. We also consider topological semantics as an alternative to relational semantics, and investigate the connection between the two. In the latter part of the course we turn our attention to more specialized logical systems and their applications, as determined by the interests of the class. Topics may include: quantified modal logic, multi-agent systems and the notion of common knowledge (with applications to game theory), temporal and dynamic logics for (nondeterministic) program execution, logics for reasoning about counterfactuals, public announcement logic, deontic logic, intuitionistic logic, and others.

80-736.name: Ethical AI in the Wild
80-736.desc: Ethical AI in the Wild is a team-taught, cross-college listed summative core course for the AI & Ethics Certificate Program at CMU. Following your completion or concurrent coursework in Ethics, AI/ML and Philosophy, this course will provide the runway for you to apply your integrative learnings to a real-world project design process for non-profit, commercial or government clients that we will align with the course calendar. You will work in teams with your customer to understand their needs in regards to the ethical considerations that influence AI integrative design, AI deployment or communication not customers regarding the use of boundary conditions of AI technologies in functional systems. Working in teams, you will apply your skills and talents to create roadmaps for AI deployment and AI communication that satisfy the business needs of your customer while also adhering to your own principles regarding the ethical use and deployment of AI across all key considerations, from privacy and agency to power relationships, equity and justice considerations. The course will culminate in final presentations, attended by our clients, in which teams will share their process and their final artifacts with the whole class and with visitors.

33-432.name: Galaxies
33-432.desc: This undergraduate course introduces the phenomenology of galaxies ranging from the smallest ‘dwarf’ galaxies to the largest galaxy clusters, highlighting the physical processes and computational/analysis tools necessary to investigate and understand the formation, evolution, and structure of galactic systems as well as their importance for adjacent areas of astrophysics.

33-732.name: Galaxies
33-732.desc: This graduate course examines the phenomenology of galaxies ranging from the smallest ‘dwarf’ galaxies to the largest galaxy clusters, highlighting the physical processes and computational/analysis tools necessary to investigate and understand the formation, evolution, structure of galactic systems as well as their importance for adjacent areas of astrophysics. Students will develop analytical, numerical, and computational problem-solving skills essential for graduate research on galaxies and related fields.

33-735.name: Professional Development for Astronomy and Astrophysics
33-735.desc: This course supports the academic, research, and career development of graduate students in astronomy and astrophysics. Students will strengthen their scientific writing, oral communication, and critical analysis through weekly activities such as seminars, journal clubs, and writing sessions. The course also provides guidance on publishing research papers, applying for fellowships, navigating the postdoctoral application process, and exploring career opportunities in academia and industry. Early and active engagement in professional development will help students build strong research portfolios and become competitive candidates for postdoctoral and industry positions.

85-403.name: Data Science for Psychology and Neuroscience
85-403.desc: This course will cover advanced topics in statistics and experimental design necessary for applied research in modern psychology, including information design, exploratory data analysis, data visualization, nonparametric statistics, data and inference errors (multicollinearity, overfitting, Simpson's and Robinson's paradox), sanitization (data anonymization, de-identification), and linear models (including conditional process models). Students will get hands on experience with simulating, analyzing, and visualizing data in the R statistical environment.

85-416.name: Applications of Cognitive Science
85-416.desc: The famous psychologist George Miller once said that Psychology should "give itself away."  The goal of this course is to look at cases where we have done so -- or at least tried.  The course focuses on applications that are sufficiently advanced as to have made an impact outside of the research field per se.  That impact can take the form of a product,  a change in practice, or a legal statute. The application should have a theoretical base, as contrasted, say, with pure measurement research as in ergonomics. Examples of applications are virtual reality (in vision, hearing, and touch), cognitive tutors based on models of cognitive processing, phonologically based reading programs, latent semantic analysis applications to writing assessment, and measurses of consumers' implicit attitudes.    The course will use a case-study approach that considers a set of applications in detail, while building a general understanding of what it means to move research into the applied setting.  The questions to be considered include:  What makes a body of theoretically based research applicable?  What is the pathway from laboratory to practice?  What are the barriers - economic, legal, entrenched belief or practice?  The format will emphasize analysis and discussion by students.  If pre reqs are not met, please reach out to the instructor for special permission to enroll.

85-433.name: Infant development: Inside the Mind of Babies
85-433.desc: This course will provide an overview of development in infancy with a focus on the emerging mind. A basic knowledge of developmental issues is assumed. We will cover the key aspects of infancy but with a primary focus on perception (seeing), cognition (thinking), and action (doing). Each week, students will be required to read a chapter in a textbook as well as short advanced empirical paper, often with conflicting accounts of a phenomenon. The instructor will introduce the key concepts, issues, and lines of research, but in each case students are expected to take an active role in discussing and developing ideas about the topic under consideration. Research methods specific to the study of infant development will be emphasized. Major issues that will be discussed include theories of developmental change, continuity in development, the nature of the psychological mechanism that underpin change, the relative contributions of heredity and environment, and the notion that all change occurs through a series of development cascades.

85-434.name: Gender, Development, Brain & Cognition
85-434.desc: This seminar takes a critical look at scientific claims about gender differences in cognition and development. We will examine the evidence behind popular and academic assertions about how girls and boys, women and men, think and learn — and how their brains function. Through readings and discussion, students will explore how empirical findings, statistical methods, and cultural assumptions intersect in the study of gender and mind. The course emphasizes close reading and reflection on how science both shapes and is shaped by social views of gender.

85-471.name: How the Brain Makes Meaning
85-471.desc: Conceptual knowledge underpins all aspects of everyday experience, from language, to thinking, to recognizing familiar objects, people and places. This seminar will survey major theories and findings about how the brain represents 'meaning.' The course will emphasize research using neuropsychological methods in brain-damaged patients and functional neuroimaging in healthy participants. Students will read primary empirical and theoretical review articles to develop an understanding of both classic findings and recent discoveries about how the human brain represents meaning.

85-809.name: Crosscultural
85-809.desc: Human beings share a common genetic inheritance, but our cultural institutions differ in a bewildering variety of ways. This course explores the many different cultural expressions of basic human cognitive and social abilities and needs, We will look at cultural variations in child rearing, mother-child attachment, language socialization, categorization, reasoning, problem-solving, architecture, music, politics, warfare, food-gathering, sex roles, mental disorders, and altered states of consciousness, all with the goal of understanding how the shape of social systems and symbolic expression reflects the economic and adaptive needs of the culture and its people. Among the approaches to these phenomena we will consider are symbolic interaction, cognitive anthropology, dialectic materialism, and modern ethnology.

The course focuses on applications that are sufficiently advanced as to have made an impact outside of the research field per se. 85-852.name: Attitudes and Persuasion
85-852.desc: This advanced undergraduate course will focus on the topic of attitude change and how various persuasive techniques are used to shape human response. The dynamics of propaganda and what makes the techniques effective on social and consumer decisions will be addressed.  The primary goals of the course are to 1) understand the dynamics of attitude change; 2) explore the mechanism by which attitude change techniques operate and 3) examine relevant theories and research in persuasion.  Examples of topics covered include the origins of attitudes, how attitudes influence judgments, social power and attitude change, and how individual decisions are influenced by the mass media.   Classic and contemporary research in the area of persuasion will be examined in the form of course readings and assignments.

85-871.name: How the Brain Makes Meaning
85-871.desc: Conceptual knowledge underpins all aspects of everyday experience, from language, to thinking, to recognizing familiar objects, people and places. This seminar will survey major theories and findings about how the brain represents 'meaning.' The course will emphasize research using neuropsychological methods in brain-damaged patients and functional neuroimaging in healthy participants. Students will read primary empirical and theoretical review articles to develop an understanding of both classic findings and recent discoveries about how the human brain represents meaning.

90-873.name: Local Policy Power, Context, and Impact
90-873.desc: Have you ever wondered why some cities, like Washington, D.C., have thousands of permitted dockless electric scooters, while Pittsburgh once had 1,000 and now has zero? Cities and towns across the country are experimenting with bold policy initiatives. A new bike network promises safe travel for all ages, a climate plan commits to cutting emissions, and a housing ordinance seeks to protect affordability. Local nonprofits mobilize for equity, business groups push for growth, and community members raise their voices in debates about who benefits and who bears the costs. But while the announcements are ambitious, the outcomes often depend on a simple set of questions: Who is the champion? What is the context? What impact will it have?  This course equips students with the frameworks, tools, and experiences needed to turn local policy into action. We will examine the political, financial, and community contexts that shape decision-making; study the role of champions in advancing initiatives; and practice measuring both the positive and negative impacts of local policies. While every place is unique- many of the variables that influence decision-making and investment are shared. Nobody has all of the answers- but this course will teach students how to ask the right questions and how decisions are made in the absence of perfection. Students will learn to anticipate risks and design strategies to make initiatives succeed, while also mapping out the roles of local governments, nonprofits, and business improvement districts. Case studies—including a comparison of Washington, DC and Pittsburgh—will ground these lessons in real-world practice. Instruction will combine interactive lectures, discussions, and applied exercises, with assessments modeled on professional practice: policy memos, stakeholder engagement maps, and impact analyses.
90-873.department: Public Policy & Mgt:Sch of Pub Pol & Mgt

90-915.name: Econometric Theory and Methods I
90-915.department: Public Policy & Mgt:Sch of Pub Pol & Mgt

16-199.name: Robotics in the Real World
16-199.desc: According to science fiction, robots should be everywhere by now. Where are they? When will we have robot pets? Where's the robot that will clean my house? Why do autonomous vehicles make mistakes? In reality, robotic systems are already here and quite capable, but not in the way storytellers predicted. This course will examine where robots are working well, why they are working well, and where things are heading. The course will compare fictional robots, robot products, and research robots to develop a better understanding of real robotic systems. Students will be expected to review case study materials in advance of classroom discussions. Additional outside work includes homework, quizzes, class participation, and a team project. No engineering or programming skills are required. This course is not intended for students pursuing a robotics degree (e.g., robotics minor, additional major in robotics, BS in robotics). This course can be taken concurrently with 16-161 or 16-467.

16-281.name: General Robotics
16-281.desc: This course presents an overview of robotics in practice and research with topics including vision, motion planning, mobile mechanisms, kinematics, inverse kinematics, and sensors. Self-paced collaborative lab projects will complement the weekly lectures. Whereas the lectures emphasize the underlying math and algorithms of each sub-discipline of robotics, the projects will emphasize the pragmatic facets of implementing robotic and mechatronic devices. The labs give students an education that go well beyond robotics into fields like control, embedded systems, programming, signal processing, interfacing, and electronics. Students usually work in teams of three: an electrical engineer, a mechanical engineer, and a computer scientist. Groups are typically self-formed except for the first lab. This course will also expose students to some of the contemporary happenings in robotics, including current robotics research, applications, and robot contests. Labs will primarily be implemented with MotorGo Plink and LEGO Mindstorm kit.

16-703.name: Fundamentals of Robot Control
16-703.desc: This graduate-level mini-course offers an introducSon to the fundamentals of control theory. Designed as part of the "Thinking about AcSon" core curriculum area, the course aims to give students an understanding of the value and applicaSons of control in roboScs. The course equips students with foundaSonal knowledge and pracScal skills needed for further self-study and for collaboraSng with experts in the area. Students will learn core concepts in control, opSmizaSon, and esSmaSon, and see how they are applied in research examples from different roboScs domains. The course is delivered through lectures, and student comprehension is assessed with three assignments that combine pracScal implementaSon problems and reviews of related research literature.

16-704.name: Fundamentals of Mechatronics Design for Robotics
16-704.desc: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of robotic hardware and mechatronic system design. Through hands-on labs and projects, students will design and analyze core subsystems such as electronic circuits, actuator control, and embedded microcontroller programming in C. Emphasis is placed on component selection, integration of sensing, actuation, and mechanical design for building robust, reproducible systems. Students will also gain experience debugging hardware, sourcing commercial components, and working collaboratively in interdisciplinary teams to develop deployable robotic systems.

16-705.name: Fundamentals of Computer Vision
16-705.desc: This course introduces the fundamental concepts and methods of computer vision—the analysis of images to reconstruct and understand the scenes that generated them. The course emphasizes practical understanding of modern computer vision pipelines as they arise in robotics and real-world applications.  Topics span low-level image processing, geometry-based 3D reconstruction methods, learning-based approaches for semantic tasks, and motion-based methods for video analysis. The course is designed to provide graduate students with a structured foundation in computer vision, enabling them to reason about representation, geometry, and inference in visual systems and to apply these ideas in robotics research.  The course is intended for graduate students who want a working and conceptual understanding of computer vision methods used in robotics and embodied AI systems.

16-736.name: Ethical AI in the Wild
16-736.desc: Ethical AI in the Wild is a team-taught, cross-college listed summative core course for the AI & Ethics Certificate Program at CMU. Following your completion or concurrent coursework in Ethics, AI/ML and Philosophy, this course will provide the runway for you to apply your integrative learnings to a real-world project design process for non-profit, commercial or government clients that we will align with the course calendar.  You will work in teams with your customer to understand their needs in regards to the ethical considerations that influence AI integrative design, AI deployment or communication not customers regarding the use of boundary conditions of AI technologies in functional systems.   Working in teams, you will apply your skills and talents to create roadmaps for AI deployment and AI communication that satisfy the business needs of your customer while also adhering to your own principles regarding the ethical use and deployment of AI across all key considerations, from privacy and agency to power relationships, equity and justice considerations. The course will culminate in final presentations, attended by our clients, in which teams will share their process and their final artifacts with the whole class and with visitors.

16-832.name: Special Topic: Integrated Planning and Learning
16-832.desc: Planning has always been one of the central components in autonomy stacks of robotic systems, ranging from self-driving vehicles and autonomous drones to mobile manipulation platforms and quadrupeds to multi-agent robotic systems. Learning-based control such as Deep RL and Imitation Learning has also emerged as one of the powerful, and potentially alternative, approaches to controlling various robotic systems, especially the ones that need to interact with their environment. These two methodologies to robot control have their own strengths and weaknesses but are often complementary. Planning provides strong guarantees on performance and safety but can be computationally intensive and depends heavily on the quality of a model, which is often hard to attain when interaction with environment is involved. Learning-based control is often faster and removes dependency on a model but depends heavily on the adequacy of the training data. This complementarity of the approaches leads to strong interest in combining them, both within academia and industry.   This class studies the latest algorithmic approaches to integrated planning and learning. In particular, the class first examines different reasons for combining the two methodologies, from computational reasons to model dependency to the duration of the development cycle of a fielded robotic system.   It then studies state-of-the-art research within each group of algorithmic approaches to integrating  planning and learning.  The course will be structured to have several classes where the instructor teaches the material. The rest of the class, students will be asked to present papers from the list compiled by the instructor. In addition, students will conduct a semester-long research project in the area of integrated planning and learning. The project is supposed to lead to a research paper worthy of publication at a top-tier robotics venue.

07-280.name: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning I
07-280.desc: This course provides an integrated introduction to artificial intelligence and machine learning that bridges core AI methods with modern approaches. Students develop both theoretical mastery and practical expertise by combining foundational concepts with the construction of influential AI systems. The curriculum covers foundational materials in search, machine learning, reinforcement learning, and probability. Students then build on these to construct detailed implementations of landmark AI systems such as AlexNet, GPT-2, and AlphaZero. This rigorous approach develops the analytical skills needed to build the future AI. Finally, as an essential component, this course will address the ethics and responsible development of AI/ML technology and products. The course emphasizes both technical excellence and ethical considerations in AI development. It serves as the foundation for 07-380 Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning II, which explores advanced topics, research methods, and specialized applications.

88-140.name: Introduction to Sociology
88-140.desc: This course offers a foundation in the study of human groups. It presents a sampling of the fundamental concepts and theories that comprise the discipline of sociology. These concepts serve as tools for the analysis of social inequality, social institutions and social change.

88-270.name: AI and Social Upheaval
88-270.desc: Over the next several decades, advances in artificial intelligence are likely to transform our societies, economies, cultures, and understanding of what it means to be human. Not enough people have begun to grapple with this fact, and with the wide range of philosophical, ethical, and political issues it raises. This course moves from foundational questions about AI's nature to practical and political concerns about its impact on our collective future. Based on the latest research spanning behavioral science, computer science, philosophy, and computational social science, we will examine the promises and pitfalls of AI, with particular emphasis on (1) the strange and difficult-to-imagine consequences of AI (i.e., second- and third-order effects) and (2) phenomena with consequences for human well-being (information ecosystems, warfare, interpersonal relationsips, scientific discovery, democracy.

88-338.name: Market Design
88-338.desc: Markets are powerful tools for organizing economic activity and distributing economic gains, but they often raise questions about fairness, ethics, and the limits of relying on prices alone. This course introduces students to the field of market design—a branch of economics that asks how rules, institutions, and incentives can be structured to achieve better social outcomes. By discussing historical examples and cutting-edge problems, as well as engaging in market experiments in class, students will learn about markets ranging from medical residency matching to auction design and voting systems. Students will explore and actually experience when markets work well on their own, when they fail, and how thoughtful design can help.  The course blends conceptual understanding with light formal modeling, helping students reason rigorously about efficiency, equity, and the role of information in economic systems. Alongside theory, students will examine real-world successes and failures, engaging with ethical dilemmas such as the repugnance of certain transactions, the tradeoffs between efficiency and fairness, and the consequences of imperfect information. By the end, students will be able to critically analyze and propose market rules in settings where "natural" outcomes may fall short of society's goals.

88-897.name: SDS Graduate Program Independent Research
88-897.desc: only for PhD students in Social and Decision Sciences

36-733.name: Advanced Statistical Learning Theory  I
36-733.desc: Focuses on deep learning theory, covering topics such as generalization, implicit regularization, benign overfitting, and optimization efficiency, guided by "Deep Learning: A Statistical Viewpoint" by Bartlett, Montanari, and Rakhlin (Acta Numerica, 2021).

36-734.name: Topics in Learning Theory II
36-734.desc: This mini explores bandit algorithms and online learning, foundational to reinforcement learning and the fine-tuning of large language models. The main reference is Lattimore and Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms (Cambridge University Press, 2020).  Additional readings may include Six Lectures on Linearized Neural Networks (Misiakiewicz & Montanari), Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms (Agarwal et al.), and A Mathematical Perspective on Transformers (Geshkovski et al.).  This sequence is intended for advanced PhD students in statistics and machine learning seeking a rigorous understanding of the statistical foundations of deep and online learning.

36-762.name: Advanced Theory I
36-762.desc: Outliers constitute a major challenge in any statistical estimation procedure: a tiny fraction of outliers in the training data could considerably change the algorithm's output. As the dimensionality of the data increases, tackling outliers becomes increasingly more challenging. This course will be an introduction to the field of robust statistics, which aims to develop statistical methods that are robust to tiny contaminations in the data. Our primary focus will be on the statistical and computational challenges that arise when the dimensionality of the data increases. This course will be theory-oriented. Prerequisites: concentration inequalities, linear algebra, and convex optimization. References: (i) Robust Statistics by P. Huber and E. Ronchetti and (ii) Algorithmic High-Dimensional Robust Statistics by Ilias Diakonikolas and Daniel M. Kane

36-763.name: Advanced Theory II
36-763.desc: A natural property that we want from an estimation procedure is stability: a small change in the training data should not lead to drastic challenges in the algorithm's output.Over the years, various notions of algorithmic stability have been proposed such as robustness to outliers, robustness to heavy-tailed data, differential privacy, and replicability. While these notions appear to encode different notions of stability prima facie, it has been observed that, surprisingly, these notions are intimately related. In this course, we will study these notions and understand the formal connections between these notions. This course will be theory-oriented and will follow many recent papers in the area.

98-299.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Making your First Indie Animation
98-299.desc: Animation, with all its nuts and bolts, can be an intimidating craft for beginners. Through this class, I hope to demolish that mental barrier-to-entry and get you started!  Ever want to see your favorite manga character in motion? Have original characters you want to bring to life? Well, this is the class for you!  Taught by a self-taught ex-beginner, this class aims to help animation enthusiasts and non-animator artists get started on their very first fully rendered piece of 2D, digital animation.   Through a semester-long project, students will be taught basic skills required to navigate the 2D animation pipeline: world-building, character design, storyboarding, 2D animation, clean-up work, post-production and many more!  There are no pre-requisites for this course, though pre-existing drawing skills and prior experience in digital illustration is recommended!

98-391.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Introduction to Honor of Kings
98-391.desc: The purpose of this class is to deepen the students' understanding of the Honor of Kings, including skills of heroes, roles, equipment build, and gameplay communication etc. By the end of this course, students should understand the foundational knowledge to play solo or in a team. This class is for both players and beginners. The first few classes would be lecture-based, but after it's going to be mainly based on actual gameplay.

98-392.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Writing Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Horror
98-392.desc: Fiction comes in a lot of different genres from realistic and speculative, each with their own elements that make the genre. This course covers at three of the most popular genres of speculative fiction: science fiction, fantasy, and horror, their elements, and how to write them in a short story format. Students will be asked to write two short stories through the semester between the three genres, and in class we will do exercises, have brief lectures and discussions, and do critiques of each other’s work to aid with the story-writing process.

98-393.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Introduction to MATLAB
98-393.desc: This course makes students familiar with MATLAB and its practical applications in future academic and industry endeavors in science and engineering. The topics include:   1. Basic MATLAB Syntax, Operations, and Data Types;  2. 2D and 3D Plotting in MATLAB;  3. Matrix Operations in MATLAB;  4. Solving Algebraic Equations in MATLAB;  5. Solving Differential Equations in MATLAB;  6. Symbolic Math in MATLAB and Comparison with Numeric Math;  7. MATLAB Control Flow and Debugging;  8. Real World Applications of MATLAB.   Students will complete several programming assignments to gain familiarity with course topics in preparation for a final project on a topic of their choice. (This course is not affiliated with MathWorks)

98-394.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Science and Its Rules: Past, Present, Future
98-394.desc: The course Science and Its Rules: Past, Present, Future invites students to explore how scientific thinking and practices are created, tested, and revised. The course combines short historical perspectives with discussions about contemporary challenges such as AI, publishing pressures, and ethics. Through a flipped-classroom, discussion-based format, students will build critical thinking, communication, and collaborative skills while reflecting on how knowledge is produced and maintained.

53-656.name: Arduino Introduction
53-656.desc: This practical course is designed to quickly take students from beginner to a basic understanding of the Arduino micro-controllers. You can expect to learn a) how to write and upload simple code for the Arduino to perform basic logic functions like reading a switch to change a motor's direction, b) how to integrate a variety of physical inputs including knobs, distance sensors, and light sensors, c) how to integrate a variety of physical outputs such as motors, lights, and speakers, and d) how to put all of these together to build simple self-contained low-cost low-power systems. The course culminates in students producing an artful and/or functional interactive creation of their own design. There are no technical prerequisites.

53-777.name: Physical Computing: Fundamentals
53-777.desc: Have you ever wanted to bring your digital ideas into the physical world—to make something you can touch, press, or wear? In this course, you'll learn how to build full systems, with computation, electronics, and materials coming together. You will explore the fundamentals of fabrication (such as laser cutting and 3D printing) and physical computing (including sensors, actuators, and microcontrollers). Through readings, discussions, and hands-on lab work, you'll gain both conceptual understanding and technical fluency in designing and building interactive physical systems. By the end of the semester, you will have prototyped several projects that blend hardware, software, and fabrication—culminating in a final piece of your own design. No prior experience is required, and this class can be taken as a complement to Mini-3: Introduction to Arduino!

90-826.name: Education Policy and Reform in the U.S.
90-826.desc: This course will provide an overview of the central ideas of education policy reform in the United States. We will examine policy decisions at the local, state, and federal levels and their impacts on learning and teaching. Guiding this course, there are two main objectives:  1. To build a framework for how policies of various types may support or hinder teaching and learning in K-12 classrooms - through which mechanism do policies affect the classroom?  2. To critically explore evidence concerning the effects of policies on teaching and learning - what is the impact on the classroom?  To understand the relationship between policy decisions and classroom success, we survey topics such as school governance and choice, school accountability, curriculum and standards reform, teacher and principal workforce, and school resources. In addition to the local, state, and federal policies that address these topics, this class will also explore recent research evaluating these policies.  To further explore the viability of these policy reforms and their likelihood of bringing about lasting and positive change to classrooms across the country, we will spend time comparing and evaluating the analytic methods and research designs that investigate the impacts of policies on student learning outcomes and teaching practice. Due to the decentralized nature of the United States education system, we will supplement our impact evaluation evidence base with robust qualitative and descriptive work to evaluate the generalizability of each policy to different contexts.
90-826.department: Public Policy & Mgt:Sch of Pub Pol & Mgt

98-395.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Principles of Jewelry Designing
98-395.desc: This course will introduce students to the fundamental concepts, techniques, and creative processes involved in jewelry design. Students will explore the basic techniques for drawing jewelry, study materials, and analyze current industry trends. By the end of the course, they will have built a strong foundation in design thinking and creative expression.

98-486.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): The Business of Sports
98-486.desc: The Business of Sports explores how modern sports organizations operate at the intersection of performance and profit. The course covers fundamentals of managing sports clubs under budget constraints, the role of analytics, and key economic concepts such as diminishing marginal returns. Through cases like Moneyball, Formula 1, and the failed European Super League, students will analyze trade-offs between profitability and sporting essence. The course also expands globally, studying strategies in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and China, while addressing contracts, sponsorships, and multi-club ownership. A structured debate and guest lecture capstone the course, alongside a final project where students design strategic plans for real-world clubs.

98-487.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Intro to Adobe After Effects
98-487.desc: Intro to Adobe After Effects is a beginner-friendly course that provides a comprehensive overview of motion graphics and visual effects. Students will learn interface and workflow basics, keyframe animation, text and shape animation, compositing, and rendering. Through hands-on projects, they will create dynamic animated videos and build their first portfolio pieces. The midterm challenges students to produce a 20–30 second animated explainer video, while the final project allows them to design a polished, creative motion graphics piece of their choice. By the end of the course, students will be able to confidently use After Effects to create professional-quality animations for presentations, branding, and storytelling.

98-488.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): The Language of Hands: ASL Foundations
98-488.desc: An interactive beginner-level course in American Sign Language (ASL) that introduces basic vocabulary, fingerspelling, grammar, facial expressions, and classifiers, while also engaging with Deaf culture and history. Students will complete weekly video homework to practice expressive and receptive skills, participate in peer-to-peer activities, and gain cultural awareness. A midterm expressive/receptive assessment and a creative ASL video project serve as the main evaluations. No prior ASL knowledge required.

98-489.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Decoding Hidden Messages in Media
98-489.desc: This interactive course explores how creators hide secret codes, easter eggs, and ciphers across media such as video games, cartoons, and web series. Students learn to decode text ciphers (Caesar, Atbash, Vigenère), image manipulations, and audio distortions. Assignments include weekly decoding tasks, a midterm in-class exam, and a final project analyzing a coded video. By the end of the course, students will be able to independently recognize and decode hidden messages.

12-614.name: Special Topics  Environmental Life Cycle Assessment
12-614.desc: Environmental impacts of construction materials and techniques are of  increasing concern to developers and building owners.  This project  will assess the environmental impact of the use of steel and wood in  construction using traditional product designs and optimized (new)  product designs. The project course will involve some in-class  lectures to familiarize students with the concept of life cycle  assessment, with steel and wood manufacturing and production  processes, with structural building design, and with construction  management processes.  Students will participate in field trips to  steel and wood manufacturing facilities. Students will work in a  multi-disciplinary team to evaluate the different materials and  structural design options, to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions  of the options, and to propose material and design choices for the  construction industry.  The goals of the course include exposing  undergraduate students to multi-disciplinary teamwork, to the  relationships between various engineering fields in decision-making  for a final product design, to environmental impacts as a design  constraint, and to the concept of life cycle assessment.    Notes: cross-listed with 27-566 section B only

24-423.name: Renewable Energy Engineering
24-423.desc: Introduction to engineering principles of various renewable energy systems, including the following topics: background on climate change and carbon sequestration, engineering analysis of renewable energy systems such as solar photovoltaic, (solar thermal), wind power, hydropower, wave energy, bio mass energy, geothermal energy, and hydrogen based fuel cells.  In addition, transitional energy systems such as nuclear power and advanced combined cycles will be introduced.  Both engineering performance and present state of development will be discussed.  Students will review and present their progress on various subjects, which will be selected based on personal interest.

24-646.name: Special Topics:Energy Technology Environmental Control Systems
24-646.desc: A critical component of energy technology design and operation is the control of environmental emissions. This course will cover the design basics of technologies used to control air and water pollution from energy conversion processes, such as power plants and industries. Technologies such as scrubbers, catalytic processes, precipitators, membranes etc will be designed. Relevant concepts from thermodynamics, mass and energy balances, mass and heat transfer and chemical reaction equilibrium and kinetics are covered. Through assignments and projects, the students will design individual pollution control technologies and then analyze their feasibility when integrated into specific applications. Preliminary cost assessment modeling will also be introduced.

48-627.name: Exploring "Afterlives" as Architectural Practice
48-627.desc: This course invites students to think differently about the sites they engage with. Building on Saidiya Hartman’s conceptualization of the “afterlives of slavery”, which gets at the endurance of the plantation in the present day, this course will help students think through ways the (often unseen) histories of a site might continue to impact the present and future. In short, this course asks: In what ways do the socio-political, ecological, and/or economic histories of a particular place continue to manifest through the built environment and how might this inform your architectural practice?   This is a reading and discussion intensive course. We will engage with works from, for example, critical geographies, the architectural humanities, and environmental studies. The course will culminate in a final project where students can choose a site where they will investigate its “afterlives.” We will discuss various methodological approaches to conducting this kind of research (including GIS, archival work, and visualizations).

14-710.name: Special Topics: The Technology Behind Information Control
14-710.desc: This course provides a comprehensive overview of internet censorship and information control in the digital age through five interconnected, module-based units.  The first module will begin by examining how the design of internet protocols can be leveraged to implement information control, providing students with a technical foundation on key protocols including HTTP(S), DNS, TCP/IP, and BGP. In the second module, we will study real-world implementations of censorship through case studies, exploring mechanisms deployed in the wild and studied by researchers. We will also look at policy triggers for censorship and internet shutdowns and analyze their collateral effects.  Module three will shift focus to circumvention methods, introducing students to tools like VPNs, proxies, and Tor, and then proceeding to advanced mechanisms like decoy routing, pluggable transports, and traffic obfuscation techniques. The fourth module will examine content filtering and algorithmic techniques used to implement content moderation and combat hate speech and abuse, while also exploring how these same technologies can be used to control online speech or enable politically motivated censorship.  The final module of the course will dive into broader societal questions including internet governance and how national borders interact with a borderless internet, the balance between privacy and law enforcement needs, and surveillance capitalism's impacts on society.  Throughout each module, students will work on take-home assignments and projects, participate in in-class discussions, and present research done in this space. From time to time, there will also be guest lectures from leading experts in the field. While no prior knowledge of computer networking is required, students are expected to read extensive technical and policy-based literature and consult supplemental resources to strengthen their understanding as needed.

54-817.name: Design Collaboration Project
54-817.desc: This course is intended to provide students with hands-on experience in the process of collaboration on a design for a production. Students in the course will work in teams to design a hypothetical production of a given play.

18-760.name: Design Quest: AgTech
18-760.desc: This course joins technical skillsets to agricultural systems within an applied, project-based course. Agriculture offers a vast design space of climate and material, resource diversity, data and energy systems, with productive real-world constraints and opportunities for innovation. Students may work in embedded electronics, energy infrastructure, data analysis, computational methods, material prototyping, and so on, acquiring or deepening skills to develop functional, site-responsive outputs. Projects could include, as examples: agricultural robotic components, digital platforms, closed-loop embedded control systems for navigation or distribution, energy storage and grid research, targeted remineralization of materially graded soil.
