Design Quest follows a collaborative, studio-style format, supporting iterative development across digital and physical platforms. Here, projects are considered as world-building processes entering a site of biological production, ecological cohabitation, and regenerative potential. Case studies ranging from microbial fermentation chambers to satellite-regulated orchards, from collapsed experiments in ag-tech to emerging logics of vertical containment explore questions of land, food, labor, and automation.  This course is cross-listed with 18360. Although students in 18360 will share lectures and most assignments with students in 18760, students in 18760 will engage in more advanced projects with a higher degree of resolution or involvement compared to students in 18360.  This course requires instructor permission. Interested students must contact Professor Chang.

49-455.name: Independent Study
49-455.desc: This independent study is designed to give undergraduate students an opportunity to explore pertinent subjects through faculty directed reading or research. Variable hrs. Restricted to EDIE students.

85-270.name: Computational Approaches for Neuroscience Questions
85-270.desc: To understand the complex dynamics of the brain and mind, neuroscientists increasingly rely on interdisciplinary computational strategies. In this course, we will introduce quantitative tools for interpreting neural data (e.g., principal component analysis, regression) and techniques for modeling neural responses (e.g., biophysical simulations, network models). Students should have a basic familiarity with programming and matrix algebra, as the course will also review foundational mathematical techniques (e.g., linear algebra, differential equations) with a focus on their application to neuroscience and cognitive science. Students will work through exercises simulating neural responses, characterizing properties of visual and auditory neurons, and building neural network classifiers.

16-992.name: Industry Practicum
16-992.desc: 16-992 Industry Practicum is a structured internship course for masters students completing a part-time internship during the academic year (fall or spring semester). Designed to integrate academic learning with real-world experience, the course enables students to apply discipline-specific knowledge, develop professional skills, explore career paths, and engage in reflective practice. Through guided reflection, students enhance their communication, teamwork, and problem-solving abilities while gaining insight into workplace dynamics and organizational culture.  Students must be physically located in Pittsburgh and may work up to 20 hours per week. The course fulfills required elective units for the MRSD & MSCV degrees and may only be completed once. Assessment includes regular check-ins, written reflections, and a final report or presentation. Students must submit an offer letter at the start of the semester and a minimum three-page summary of their internship experience at the end of the semester. International students in F-1 or J-1 status must consult with their OIE advisor regarding appropriate work authorization (CPT or pre-completion OPT).

18-244.name: Intro to ASIC and FPGA Chip Design
18-244.desc: This course is a low-barrier-to-entry introduction to chip design. The student will learn how to design, implement, emulate, and verify an ASIC chip. Along the way, the student will be exposed to many common tools and techniques in the chip-implementation area. Many of those tools focus on FPGAs for emulation and development.  For the final project in the course, students will tapeout a non-trivial digital design, to be fabricated using an open-hardware flow. It may take six to twelve months, but students will eventually end up with an actual chip that contains their design.  This course is cross listed with 18644.  Although students in 18-244 will share lectures and in-class assignments with students in 18644, those students in 18644 will be expected to complete a more challenging semester-long project.  Additionally, students in 18644 have an additional assignment, one in which they investigate a research topic and write an in-depth literature review.

18-440.name: Autonomous Robotics I
18-440.desc: This course combines machine learning and robotics in a hands-on approach that encourages discovery. The course will have three portions. First, students learn deep learning fundamentals, convolutional neural networks, and object detection. In the second portion, students learn the fundamentals of Robot Operating System 2 (ROS2). In the last portion, they learn how to implement ROS2 computational graphs and machine learning models on a hardware and software acceleration platform to achieve real-time robotic perception, cognition, and action. Students develop a miniature self-driving robot based on the Jetson Orin Nano platform and the RealSense camera for vision. Students are encouraged to discover their robotic application tasks. Prior machine learning or robotics knowledge is not required. However, strong C/Python programming skills, computer systems knowledge, and a sense of wonder are strongly preferred. This course is crosslisted with 18840. Although students in 18440 will share lectures with students in 18840, students in 18840 will be given exams and project criteria that will be more challenging than those in 18440.

18-644.name: Intro to ASIC and FPGA Chip Design
18-644.desc: This course is a low-barrier-to-entry introduction to chip design. The student will learn how to design, implement, emulate, and verify an ASIC chip. Along the way, the student will be exposed to many common tools and techniques in the chip-implementation area. Many of those tools focus on FPGAs for emulation and development.  For the final project in the course, students will tapeout a non-trivial digital design, to be fabricated using an open-hardware flow. It may take six to twelve months, but students will eventually end up with an actual chip that contains their design.  This course is cross listed with 18244.  Although students in 18244 will share lectures and in-class assignments with students in 18644, those students in 18644 will be expected to complete a more challenging semester-long project.  Additionally, students in 18644 have an additional assignment, one in which they investigate a research topic and write an in-depth literature review.

18-840.name: Autonomous Robotics I
18-840.desc: This course combines machine learning and robotics in a hands-on approach that encourages discovery. The course will have three portions. First, students learn deep learning fundamentals, convolutional neural networks, and object detection. In the second portion, students learn the fundamentals of Robot Operating System 2 (ROS2). In the last portion, they learn how to implement ROS2 computational graphs and machine learning models on a hardware and software acceleration platform to achieve real-time robotic perception, cognition, and action. Students develop a miniature self-driving robot based on the Jetson Orin Nano platform and the RealSense camera for vision. Students are encouraged to discover their robotic application tasks. Prior machine learning or robotics knowledge is not required. However, strong C/Python programming skills, computer systems knowledge, and a sense of wonder are strongly preferred. This course is crosslisted with 18840. Although students in 18440 will share lectures with students in 18840, students in 18840 will be given exams and project criteria that will be more challenging than those in 18440.

94-847.name: Responsible AI & AI Governance: Identifying and Mitigating Risks
94-847.desc: As AI and machine learning systems become integral to products and services across industries, it is critical to identify and mitigate the risks associated with their design, deployment, and operation. This course examines the evolving landscape of AI governance, exploring both technical and organizational strategies for developing trustworthy and responsible AI systems. In 2025, the course expands to cover responsible development and governance of Agentic AI—systems capable of autonomous reasoning, planning, and collaboration. Students explore governance strategies across the AI lifecycle, including model alignment (RLHF, RLAIF), fairness, differential privacy, explainability, interpretability, and AI red teaming. The course integrates evolving policy and regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, and OECD guidelines. Case studies examine responsible AI practices in foundation models, generative systems, and agent-based ecosystems. The course combines technical, policy, and management perspectives to equip students with the tools and frameworks needed to assess and mitigate AI-related risks.

14-713.name: Special Topics: Secure and Responsible AI
14-713.desc: This course addresses the dual imperatives of security and responsibility in modern AI development. Students explore how to build AI systems that are resilient against attacks while respecting privacy, promoting fairness, and maintaining transparency. The curriculum integrates technical security measures with ethical frameworks, covering topics such as adversarial machine learning, differential privacy, fairness metrics, explainable AI, adversarial robustness, bias detection and mitigation, secure model training and deployment, and reliability assurance.   Through hands-on projects, students develop AI solutions and then systematically evaluate their implementations across multiple dimensions: security vulnerabilities and defenses, reliability and performance under various conditions, ethical considerations including fairness and privacy, and overall trustworthiness for deployment. Students gain practical experience implementing security controls for machine learning pipelines, conducting fairness evaluations, assessing system reliability, and applying frameworks for building secure, ethical, reliable, and trustworthy AI systems. The course prepares students for careers developing AI systems in regulated industries and high-stakes applications where security, ethics, reliability, and trustworthiness are paramount.  This course assumes students have some working knowledge of writing AI code and developing machine learning applications. A background in security (an Intro Course) and AI (an intro course) is preferred but not required.

82-602.name: LCAL Graduate Elective
82-602.desc: This course fulfills a general elective requirement for the Masters in Applied Second Language Acquisition. Course requirements include attending an undergraduate course on a topic chosen as advised, and completing supplementary graduate-level work in consultation with the course instructor and the MA program advisor.

76-799.name: Introduction to Film Studies
76-799.desc: This course is an introduction to the history, technology, aesthetics, and ideology of film. Our main focus is the narrative fiction film, but we will also discuss documentaries, avant-garde work, and animation. The central organizing principle is historical, but there are a number of recurring thematic concerns. These include an examination of the basic principles of filmmaking, the development of film technology, the definition of film as both art and business, and the history of film as an object of critical and cultural study. The goals of this course are threefold. First, it will provide you with a solid grounding in the key issues and concepts of film studies. Second, it will expand your ability to knowledgeably critique individual cinematic works and their relationship to the larger culture. Lastly, it will provide you with experience in expressing your critiques in writing.

66-219.name: Purposeful Negotiation
66-219.desc: Negotiation is part of our daily lives. The opportunities to become a more thoughtful and skillful negotiator can have big impacts. This course is designed to immerse students in practical activities, building skills that can be used immediately for everything from managing equitable group work in teams to negotiating salaries.  The course will introduce key theories of negotiation, including distributive bargaining and interest-based negotiation. Students will learn how to plan a negotiation, incorporate their values into negotiations, interact with different parties, and adjust their planned strategy as they learn more about the conditions and context. They will also learn to select and apply appropriate tactics based on the relationships involved and the outcomes they aim to achieve. Students will have opportunities to reflect individually and collectively to assess the results of their negotiations in order to become effective negotiators in personal and professional contexts.

79-359.name: Truth, Lies, and Conspiracies
79-359.desc: Throughout the history of the United States, people have understood their lives and the world around them in many ways. Often, as political theorist Richard Hofstadter wrote, Americans have done so in "paranoid style." This course explores how Americans have argued over the "truth" since the founding of the nation and at several key moments of social and political tension through to the present. We will think critically as we seek throughlines in the long history of conspiratorial thinking that has animated so many to perceive dark plots, often elaborately conceived, behind events of the day. We will ask several key questions. Have Americans always agreed on their story? What role have facts and falsehoods played in major societal changes? How can we understand essential "truths" in American history when "lies" have always accompanied them? Students will gain historical context about what it means to live in a supposedly "post-truth era," learn how historians have approached and disagreed about the concept of "truth" in studying the past, and grapple with hard truths as we attempt to understand America's contested realities.

51-668.name: Environments Studio II
51-668.desc: The courses Environments Studio II: Designing Environments for Interaction and Prototyping Lab II: Environments run in tandem to explore the spatiotemporal interactions between people, objects and spaces. In this course you will: engage critically and reflectively with key related theories and debates; establish and shape your own knowledge, understanding and position; and deepen your design literacy and contextual awareness; develop work that is tied to what is currently happening in the design field. This is a project-based studio, so you will learn through making, designing rich interactions and spatial experiences at different levels of scale within physical, digital and hybrid environments.

51-669.name: Prototyping Lab II: Environments
51-669.desc: In this lab, you'll experiment with ways that designers can craft spaces through collective, time-based, and distributed interactions. You will learn how to: represent environments using digital drawing tools, fabricate environments using computer-controlled machines, connect environments using code and electronics, and activate environments using motion tracking and gaming platforms. You will learn how to use these technologies but also-and more importantly-how to self-learn and problem-solve as current tools evolve and new ones emerge. In other words, through this course, you will become a maker with both the skills and mindset to help you succeed in your academic and professional careers in the years to come.

84-704.name: Policy Analysis, Writing, and Presentation Skills
84-704.desc: This course will focus heavily on the production processes expected by employers. Students will gain valuable experience with policy writing and editing, developing presentation skills, and will be guided through ethical and effective research processes including the location and assessment of credible sources. A focus of this course will be on the critical evaluation of information versus disinformation and developing the communication skills necessary to inform and persuade a variety of audiences.
84-704.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

95-559.name: Cybersecurity for AI & ML
95-559.desc: This course is only for Heinz College ITLab Students. No other students will be registered for this course.

95-724.name: AI Literacy and Communication Strategies
95-724.desc: Communication is an essential element in any professional field, from the public policy area, to the medical field, the tech sector and beyond.  Writing and presenting for consulting firms, corporate entities, government agencies, think tanks, or advocacy groups differs significantly from academic contexts. Professional communication expectations are even higher for leaders in emerging fields, who will be called upon to translate complex technical content for non-expert stakeholders, to manage cross-functional teams, and communicate clear expectations, outcomes, and recommendations in a fast-paced and quickly evolving environment.  Accordingly, this course provides practical instruction for preparing and delivering professional documents and presentations in the 21st century workplace. This course challenges students to convey critical thinking by anticipating readers' needs and the perspectives of stakeholders in the practice of analyzing and shaping policy related documents and presentations related to the emerging field of AI. Students will hone a wide variety of skills integral to management-level communication, including: developing essential and persuasive content, organizing information into useful and efficient forms, targeting diverse audiences with varying levels of expertise and roles, communicating complex ideas supported by research and data, ensuring clarity, controlling tone, and designing meaningful visuals. Overall, the course helps students develop confidence and apply effective techniques when speaking in a public setting as well as producing meaningful and effective written documents.   Note: This course assumes proficiency in English grammar. Numerous resources for improving English skills are available through CMU.

49-777.name: Special Topics: AI Product Strategy & Prototyping
49-777.desc: Artificial intelligence is transforming how digital products are conceived, built, and operated. Product leaders are increasingly expected to define AI strategy, evaluate model options, assess economic trade-offs, and deliver working prototypes that demonstrate value.  This course equips students to design AI-enabled product strategies and develop functional AI prototypes. Students will learn how to identify high-value AI opportunities, evaluate technical and economic feasibility, design responsible AI systems, and build proof-of-concept solutions using modern AI platforms and APIs. The course integrates product strategy, AI capability literacy, cost modeling, risk management, and rapid prototyping into a cohesive product leadership framework.  By the end of the course, students will be able to articulate an AI strategy for a real product context and demonstrate that strategy through a working prototype supported by business, technical, and ethical analysis.

11-962.name: Introduction to Machine Learning
11-962.desc: The course introduces students to the theoretical foundation of elementary Machine Learning (ML) concepts and algorithms, with a focus on how they relate to the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Students who complete this course will be prepared for continued graduate education in the areas of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and in particular we prepare students for advanced courses in Large Language Models and related topics. Students become skilled in evaluating the machine learning models (e.g. Decision Trees, Perceptron, Neural Networks, Deep Learning) that are well suited to supervised learning tasks, unsupervised learning tasks, and reinforcement learning tasks via a first principles approach (e.g. Information Entropy to motivate Decision Tree selection). Students develop practical skills with hands on coding assignments (e.g. modeling, training, testing, hyperparameter cross validation, visualization, error analysis) embedded in every aspect of the course to balance theoretical understanding with practical skills (e.g. support Gradient Descent theory with mini-batch Stochastic Gradient Descent and scheduled learning). Students will develop science communication skills required to effectively communicate their findings via data visualization and comprehensive reporting. This is a certificate course and is only opened to certificate seeking students.

11-973.name: Foundations of Computational Data Science
11-973.desc: This course provides an introduction to foundational concepts, learning material, and projects related to the three core areas of Data Science: Computing Systems, Analytics, and Human-Centered Data Science. Students completing this class will be prepared for further graduate education in Data Science and/or Artificial Intelligence. Students acquire skills in solution design (e.g., architecture, framework APIs, cloud computing), analytic algorithms (e.g., classification, clustering, ranking, prediction), interactive analysis (Jupyter Notebook), applications to data science domains (e.g., Natural Language Processing, Computer Vision) and visualization techniques for data analysis, solution optimization, and performance measurement on real-world tasks. This course is a remote course which is designed specifically for remote students in a certificate program.

48-628.name: GeoAI: Advanced GIS for Policy and Design
48-628.desc: As cities confront climate risk and social inequity, effective policy relies on advanced spatial intelligence. This course introduces GeoAI, the integration of GIS and AI, as a framework to empower decision makers with evidence-based insights. Students will analyze satellite imagery and socioeconomic spatial data to tackle challenges, such as heat vulnerability and environmental justice. Using ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online, students will perform raster analysis, predictive modeling, and deep learning classification. Beyond technical implementation, the course focuses on how to make informed decisions by assessing bias and uncertainty. No prior coding is required; the focus remains on making complex GeoAI workflows accessible for urban planning and policy. Through hands-on activities, students will learn to communicate findings through policy-oriented maps, culminating in a final project that designs a reproducible GeoAI workflow to support real-world policy interventions and empower leadership with the tools needed to address growing urban inequities.

60-109.name: Non-Major Film: Creature Features
60-109.desc: As long as humans have existed, they have told stories of monsters: from the beasts that hunted our ancestors in the dark of the night to the creatures that lurk under the beds of children, troubling their dreams. These inhuman creations have personified our fears of nature, of difference, and of our own aberrant desires. In this course, we will watch films with murderous sharks, man-made horrors, and creatures from beyond the stars to better understand what makes a monster. To help us articulate our own relationship to monstrosity, we will read scholarship from philosophers, filmmakers, and authors who ask important questions about our continued obsession with these creatures. Are monsters defined by their physical forms? Their intentions? By audiences' anxieties? Or do they lurk within all of us?

60-122.name: Comics for Non-Majors
60-122.desc: In this course, students will learn practical and technical skills to communicate their ideas more effectively through comics and sequential art. The first half of the semester will focus on defining the language of comics, and, through a series of technical and exploratory exercises, students will learn the basic tools needed to improve/refine their visual storytelling skills. Specific challenges, such as silent-panel storytelling and modular panel layouts, will be introduced to spark curiosity and encourage students to reexamine their assumptions about the medium. In the second half of the term, students will conceptualize and execute a fully realized four-page comic or an excerpt from a larger story. In addition to creating new comics, we will explore the origins of the modern graphic novel through comic readings. Students will be exposed to both graphic and non-graphic artists whose works have challenged and redefined the genre. We will explore these artists to understand how our work draws on a rich lineage. Students will also be encouraged to think beyond the commonly accepted notions of what constitutes a comic and will ultimately be challenged to question how their perspective and voice best align with the medium.

60-166.name: Photography in the Dark
60-166.desc: This evening course is formed around a series of short projects and exercises designed to explore the processes, techniques, and concepts of photographing in the dark. Students will primarily be working at night to gain experience using both natural and artificial lighting techniques in low light. Topics and techniques that will be covered include but are not limited to post-production techniques, approaches to file-preparation and digital printing, artificial lighting experimentation, portable strobe lighting, digital and analog processes. Regular lectures and demos will provide technical starting points and contextual framework for students to complete assignments. There are no pre-requisites for this course but introductory level camera knowledge and/or completion of Digital Photography I (60/62-142) is recommended. A lab fee is charged for this course.

60-167.name: Instant Photography: The Unrepeatable Image
60-167.desc: This course will explore Instant photographic techniques and concepts to extend the boundaries of the photographic image. Through the course we will explore contemporary instant image making using Polaroid, Instax, and darkroom techniques. Subjects covered are photography techniques with instant cameras, understanding the context of unique one-of-a-kind images, instant photographic emulsions, alternative uses to Polaroid photography, and concepts and theory of the still image. As we move through the course, we will also explore the theory and history of photography, particularly from 1950 moving forward, and its many ways to create an image that are not standard in today's imaging practices. A diverse range of contemporary photographic work will be presented to increase students' visual awareness and understanding of the possibilities inherent in the medium. Through work/review sessions, students will be encouraged to evaluate their own ideas and judgments in pursuit of a well-communicated image. A lab fee is charged for this course.

60-168.name: The Infinite Roll: Cell Phone Photography
60-168.desc: Cell phones are everywhere, and photography is more accessible than ever. This course will explore cell phone photography techniques and concepts ranging from how to make the best exposure and composition to more complex subjects such as ideal and ethical uses of cell phones in photography. A major theme for the course is the investigation of how moments happen quickly and capturing them as a catalyst for good artwork. This course not only covers how best to use this tool to its optimum effect, but also how to use it as a means of expression and artistic outlet. Subjects include introductory photographic techniques (exposure, composition, form), understanding the context of photographing in a world with endless images, editing with software on phone vs. computer, and concepts of the still image. A diverse range of contemporary photographic work will be presented to increase students' visual awareness and understanding of the possibilities inherent in the medium. Through work/review sessions, students will be encouraged to evaluate their own ideas and judgments in pursuit of a well-communicated image. A lab fee is charged for this course.

60-262.name: Intermediate Studio: Metals
60-262.desc: Intermediate Metals is an intermediate studio course focused on contemporary steel fabrication techniques used in sculpture and installation-based practices. The course emphasizes hands-on learning through the development of practical skills and guided projects that introduce students to working with steel as a primary structural material. Students will learn a range of core metalworking processes, including MIG welding, metal cutting, grinding, drilling, bending, plate shearing, and plasma cutting. Instruction will cover both hot and cold fabrication methods, material preparation, joint design, structural thinking, and safe operation of equipment. Projects are designed to build technical proficiency while encouraging students to apply fabrication skills to spatial and formal problems.  The course is structured around a series of guided assignments with defined prompts and technical requirements. These projects focus on building functional and sculptural forms using steel, with increasing attention to scale, stability, and construction logic. While projects are structured, students are encouraged to explore individual ideas within each prompt and may incorporate additional non-metal materials as appropriate.  Class time includes demonstrations, supervised shop work, individual feedback, group critiques, and discussions of contemporary artists working with steel. By the end of the semester, students will have developed a strong foundational skill set in metal fabrication and the ability to confidently design and construct steel-based works for studio and exhibition contexts. A foundations sculpture course is recommended as preparation for this class.

60-266.name: Intermediate SIS: Wood
60-266.desc: Intermediate Wood is a studio course focused on contemporary woodworking techniques used in sculpture, installation, and object-based studio practices. The course emphasizes hands-on learning through guided projects that introduce students to working with wood as a primary structural and expressive material. Students will work in the School of Art wood shop and learn a range of core woodworking processes, including cutting, milling, shaping, drilling, routing, sanding, and turning. Equipment used in the course includes table saws, routers, sanders, miter saws, drill presses, planers, and the lathe, alongside a wide range of hand tools. Instruction will cover material selection, measuring and layout, joinery methods, surface finishing, and safe operation of all tools.  The course is structured around three guided projects with defined prompts and technical requirements. These assignments focus on planning and building functional and sculptural forms, emphasizing joinery, structural logic, and precision. Students will learn how to develop projects through sketches, mock-ups, and material testing, and how to combine hand processes with machine-based techniques to achieve accurate and durable constructions.  Class time includes demonstrations, supervised shop work, individual feedback, and group critiques. By the end of the semester, students will have developed a strong working knowledge of woodworking tools and processes, along with the ability to independently plan and execute wood-based projects suitable for studio and exhibition contexts. Foundations Sculpture II is recommended to be prepared for this course.

60-269.name: Intermediate Studio: Glass
60-269.desc: Melt, stretch, bend, blow. This introductory course explores the tools and processes to pursue personal expression and aesthetics with glass as the medium.   Technical instruction covers manipulation of solid glass, blowing hollow tube, and color application. In this hands-on studio course, students have ample practice time, assignments, and presentations with critique.   The goal of this course is to utilize fundamental techniques of glassworking with the torch to create sculpture and objects. Lectures and dialogue will incorporate conversation about historical and contemporary glass art.

60-282.name: Staged Photography
60-282.desc: This studio course introduces students to staged photographic practices through technical instruction, conceptual frameworks, and applied methods. The hands-on format provides experience with staging scenes, studio lighting, and tethered shooting. Students will engage with these topics through weekly presentations, discussions, assignments, workshops, and critiques. The course examines artists who critically engage with photography through constructed imagery, while encouraging experimental approaches and creative risk-taking. A lab fee is charged for this course.

60-416.name: Advanced ETB: Documentary Storytelling
60-416.desc: In this course you will be learning strategies of audio and visual storytelling in the service of documenting and sharing the astounding world that surrounds us. You will apply these strategies to produce advanced works of your own. Video production techniques will be covered, although student work will be open to any media and experimental approaches will be encouraged. The course will examine documentary works that utilize film, video, audio, photography, spoken word and object-based practice to convey complicated narratives. "Documentary" does imply non-fiction, although it is not necessarily about "objectivity" either. These works exist in the sticky, often uncomfortable, yet fascinating, relationship that human experience has to reality.

60-436.name: Advanced SIS: Digital Fabrication CNC Projects
60-436.desc: "Advanced CNC is an upper-level studio course that explores the applied use of computer-controlled cutting and routing processes within sculpture and installation-based studio practices. Students will work with a range of CNC tools, including a 3-axis CNC motion machine, a Shaper Origin handheld system, and a small-format CNC mill (Nomad 883), to design, prototype, and fabricate precise physical objects from digital files.  In this course, students will learn to use Rhino and Adobe Illustrator to generate and prepare files for CNC output, including strategies for vector drawing, 3D modeling, toolpath preparation, and material setup. Emphasis is placed on understanding the technical workflow from digital design to physical fabrication and safe use of equipment. The course is structured around three guided projects with defined prompts. These assignments are designed to build sequentially, introducing increasingly complex machining strategies while requiring students to apply CNC processes to spatial, structural, and material problems. This is not an open-ended independent studio; projects are skill-based and focused on developing technical fluency through hands-on production.  As a class, students will explore the iterative nature of CNC fabrication, including testing, revision, and problem-solving through multiple outputs. Experimentation will be emphasized through layering, assembly, and combining machine-based processes with hand fabrication methods. Students will also engage with contemporary examples of artists and designers using CNC tools as part of their regular studio practice. By the end of the semester, students will have developed a strong working knowledge of CNC workflows and the ability to integrate digital machining into a broader sculptural practice. Prior digital fabrication class experience is strongly preferred.  "

60-494.name: Advanced Studio: Critical Craft: Art, Community, and Intention
60-494.desc: This course approaches craft as a site of intention, necessity, and collective care, and as a tool for critical discourse. We will examine how craft has been used to express need, support activism, and give form to voices often excluded from dominant cultural narratives. Centering art as social practice, the course positions making as a political act—one that can redistribute resources, strengthen community, and function as a strategy for survival. Students will learn to work in context, using social practice to deepen and elevate craft by embedding meaning, responsibility, and relationship into material processes. Through collaboration, site visits, and partnerships with Pittsburgh-based makers and organizations, the course explores craft not only as an object, but as a process and a conversation that elevates the meaning and impact of exhibited work.

93-877.name: Strategic Communication for Arts and Entertainment Management
93-877.desc: This course strengthens advanced writing and speaking skills for leadership roles in museums, galleries, performing arts organizations, and entertainment enterprises. Students learn to develop strategic, data-informed communications tailored to diverse stakeholders. Through focused practice in structuring information, crafting clear and persuasive narratives, designing purposeful visuals, and presenting with confidence across in-person and remote settings, students refine their written, visual, vocal, and nonverbal communication styles. The course also addresses media engagement and the responsible use of generative AI. Collaboration is a key component of the course, supported through small-group exercises, peer feedback, and team presentations. By the end of the semester, students are prepared to produce polished professional documents and deliver strategic presentations that support decision-making.

42-618.name: Nanoscale Manufacturing Using Structural DNA Nanotechnology
42-618.desc: This project course introduces modern nanoscale manufacturing using structural nucleic acid nanotechnology with a focus on DNA-based methods. This approach to manufacturing has much in common with other fabrication methods in micro- and nano-engineering: computer aided design tools are necessary for device design, and resulting structures can only be seen using advanced microscopy. However, instead of machining larger materials down to micro- and nanostructures, DNA nanotechnology including DNA origami is fabricated using a "bottom up" approach for self-assembling individual oligonucleotides into 2D and 3D nanostructures. Resulting structures can be engineered to have novel mechanical, biochemical and electrical properties with broad-ranging applications in medicine, biological computing, and nanoelectronics. The course will include lectures, hands-on physical modeling, homework problems, 3D modeling, coarse-grained simulation, and student team projects and presentations.

42-642.name: Biomechanics of Human Movement
42-642.desc: This course provides an overview of the mechanical principles underlying human movement biomechanics and the experimental and modeling techniques used to study it. Specific topics will include locomotion, motion capture systems, force plates, muscle mechanics, musculoskeletal modeling, three dimensional kinematics, inverse dynamics, forward dynamic simulations, and imaging-based biomechanics. Homework and final class projects will emphasize applications of movement biomechanics in orthopedics, rehabilitation, and sports. ***Students are expected to have knowledge of ordinary differential equations and rigid body dynamics at the level of 24-351.***

42-662.name: Special Topics: Human Factors for Medical Device Development
42-662.desc: This course introduces human factors and ergonomics principles as applied to medical device design. Students learn anthropometry, user interface and interaction design, workplace and task analysis, hand tool design principles, and the biomechanics of work-related musculoskeletal disorders. Additional topics include human error, regulatory expectations, particularly FDA guidance on applying human factors, and methods for conducting human factors studies. Emphasis is placed on the role of human factors in product development, regulatory submissions, and risk management. Through lectures and hands-on activities, students gain practical experience analyzing device-user interactions and applying human-centered design methods. A team-based design project reinforces and integrates course concepts.

42-671.name: Special Topics: Precision Medicine for Biomedical Engineers
42-671.desc: Precision medicine seeks to move beyond one-size-fits-all treatments by targeting disease heterogeneity at the molecular-, tissue-, and patient-level. The goal of this course is to cover emerging strategies for the profiling and treatment of disease based on a patient's unique biological profile. Topics covered by this course will include (1) profiling disease heterogeneity using omics and biological sequencing, (2) disease biomarkers, (3) genetics and risk stratification, (4) electronic medical records, and (5) prognostic models and clinical decision-making. Throughout this course, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), and heart failure (HF) will be used as case studies for the application of precision medicine concepts. Machine learning and large language models will also be discussed as emerging tools for pattern extraction in various areas of precision medicine. Basic familiarity with a high-level programming language (e.g. Python, MATLAB) is preferred, though publicly available computational tools will be provided for students' usage.

45-867.name: Designing AI Products & Experiences
45-867.desc: This course introduces a human-centered approach to designing AI-powered products and experiences. We'll examine AI's capabilities and limits, and the design opportunities in user control versus automation, trust and explainability, and conversational and generative agents. The course is not about coding, but shaping AI into usable and strategically valuable products. Alongside lectures and discussions, you will design an AI-powered product—defining a human challenge, mastering UI/UX best practices, developing creative concepts, and prototyping in Figma. By the end, you will have taken an AI product from idea to a prototype, gaining powerful design tools and principles you can apply in product management, consulting, entrepreneurship, or any path where intelligent products are reshaping business.

46-964.name: Algorithm Design and Applications for Computational Finance
46-964.desc: A project-based course in which students apply advanced algorithmic techniques to computational problems in finance. The specific algorithmic content is chosen to support the semester's projects and may draw from areas such as graph algorithms, linear programming, network flow, streaming algorithms, and randomized algorithms. The course emphasizes the full arc of applied problem solving: formalizing a potentially under-specified problem, selecting and adapting appropriate algorithms, building a working system, and evaluating its performance.

70-399.name: Private Equity and Venture Capital
70-399.desc: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to both venture capital and private equity, exploring their development as industries, key participants, organizational structures, and common contract terms. Students will examine how investors create value through financial, governance, and operational engineering, as well as how performance is measured and how it relates to investor compensation. The curriculum covers essential valuation techniques—including the venture capital method and the leveraged buyout (LBO) model—alongside an analysis of common exit strategies for investments. Course Materials Note: This course may use third-party course material that is not available for individual purchase from the publisher. If so, the third-party course material will be secured and provided by the Tepper School to students enrolled in the course, and students will be required to pay the University the associated additional course materials fee. The amount of the fee is dependent on the University's cost of the particular materials provided, typically ranging from $13 to $75.

62-112.name: Introduction to 3D Print Casting
62-112.desc: This course introduces the integration of digital fabrication and glass casting processes. Students will learn foundational techniques in 3D scanning, modeling, and printing alongside mold-making strategies for translating digitally produced forms into cast glass objects. Emphasis is placed on material compatibility, mold construction, casting methods for complex three-dimensional forms, and finishing techniques. As an introductory project, students will scan their own head produce a 3D-printed model, and cast a scaled glass bust, providing a comprehensive overview of the digital-to-glass workflow. The course welcomes students new to either digital fabrication or glass, as well as those seeking to expand existing studio practices. Registration can only be done on or after your scheduled registration day. Please email Stefanie McGowan (stefanim@andrew.cmu.edu) for more information and to register. Registration is first come, first served. Course fee is $270. Class is held at Pittsburgh Glass Center. 3D Print Casting will be held from September 24, 2026 to November 19, 2026.

62-166.name: Photography in the Dark
62-166.desc: This evening course is formed around a series of short projects and exercises designed to explore the processes, techniques, and concepts of photographing in the dark. Students will primarily be working at night to gain experience using both natural and artificial lighting techniques in low light. Topics and techniques that will be covered include but are not limited to post-production techniques, approaches to file-preparation and digital printing, artificial lighting experimentation, portable strobe lighting, digital and analog processes. Regular lectures and demos will provide technical starting points and contextual framework for students to complete assignments. There are no pre-requisites for this course but introductory level camera knowledge and/or completion of Digital Photography I (60/62-142) is recommended. A lab fee is charged for this course.

62-167.name: Instant Photography: The Unrepeatable Image
62-167.desc: This course will explore Instant photographic techniques and concepts to extend the boundaries of the photographic image. Through the course we will explore contemporary instant image making using Polaroid, Instax, and darkroom techniques. Subjects covered are photography techniques with instant cameras, understanding the context of unique one-of-a-kind images, instant photographic emulsions, alternative uses to Polaroid photography, and concepts and theory of the still image. As we move through the course, we will also explore the theory and history of photography, particularly from 1950 moving forward, and its many ways to create an image that are not standard in today's imaging practices. A diverse range of contemporary photographic work will be presented to increase students' visual awareness and understanding of the possibilities inherent in the medium. Through work/review sessions, students will be encouraged to evaluate their own ideas and judgments in pursuit of a well-communicated image.  A lab fee is charged for this course.

62-168.name: The Infinite Roll: Cell Phone Photography
62-168.desc: "The best camera is the one that's with you." (Chase Jarvis)  Cell phones are everywhere, and photography is more accessible than ever. This course will explore cell phone photography techniques and concepts ranging from how to make the best exposure and composition to more complex subjects such as ideal and ethical uses of cell phones in photography. A major theme for the course is the investigation of how moments happen quickly and capturing them as a catalyst for good artwork. This course not only covers how best to use this tool to its optimum effect, but also how to use it as a means of expression and artistic outlet. Subjects include introductory photographic techniques (exposure, composition, form), understanding the context of photographing in a world with endless images, editing with software on phone vs. computer, and concepts of the still image. A diverse range of contemporary photographic work will be presented to increase students' visual awareness and understanding of the possibilities inherent in the medium. Through work/review sessions, students will be encouraged to evaluate their own ideas and judgments in pursuit of a well-communicated image. A lab fee is charged for this course.

62-282.name: Staged Photography
62-282.desc: This studio course introduces students to staged photographic practices through technical instruction, conceptual frameworks, and applied methods. The hands-on format provides experience with staging scenes, studio lighting, and tethered shooting. Students will engage with these topics through weekly presentations, discussions, assignments, workshops, and critiques. The course examines artists who critically engage with photography through constructed imagery, while encouraging experimental approaches and creative risk-taking. A lab fee is charged for this course.

84-301.name: Policy & Persuasion
84-301.desc: This skills based class will focus on how to identify policy problems, develop solutions, and build the case for them, for a range of audiences. Students will choose a topic, research it, and learn how to develop succinct, memorable descriptions of policy problems for experts and lay audiences. Students will learn how to develop and edit policy briefings, white papers, op-eds, infographics, action memos, prepare for Congressional testimony, and other short form writing around their chosen topic. The goal of this course is to prepare students to engage in policy discussions both within organizations, and with the broader public debate.
84-301.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

84-345.name: Hackers, the Law, & Policy Responses
84-345.desc: As the internet has developed, individuals have tested the bounds of acceptable behavior, engaging in activities that have caused disruption, harm, or otherwise infringed on established rights. As these disruptions -- real and potential -- were discovered, policy makers have reacted to them by establishing new rules to direct, limit, or outlaw the behaviors that led to the disruption. In this class, we will review foundational hacking cases and examine the policy debates that flowed from them, and the ways in which laws and policies changed in response to understand the frameworks and legal limitations we operate within today.
84-345.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

84-358.name: Money, Connections, and Power: Interests and Influence in the US
84-358.desc: Pundits and politicians on both sides of the aisle decry the influence of special interests and lobbyists, but who exactly are these entities, and how much power do they actually possess? This course explores the range of actors who seek to impact policymaking in the US, including individuals, issue groups, unions, businesses, social movements, and subnational governments, along with the means they employ. We will begin by considering whose interests are reflected in the outcomes of the political process and whose are not. To explain these disparities, the class will examine the major non-electoral avenues of influence in US politics, in particular lobbying, donating to campaigns, mobilizing a membership base, and supplying expertise to politicians. For each of these topics, students will analyze real-world data to determine who engages in these behaviors, how they do so, and what effects their activity has.
84-358.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

84-497.name: Undergraduate Research Mini
84-497.desc: Students conduct research under the supervision of a faculty member. Students who wish to engage in research should seek out a faculty member whose interests are appropriate to the research. Prerequisite: Students must also complete an "Independent Study/Research for Credit" form, available from the Deputy Director for Academic Affairs or on the CMIST website. Permission of a faculty sponsor.
84-497.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

84-601.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

84-630.name: Race for the Future: US-China Tech Competition
84-630.desc: The US and China both aspire to maintain the lead in global technological development. But each has a very different approach to building technologies and incentivizing innovation. This course will focus on key developing technology areas -- AI, cyber, semiconductors, space, and military technologies. It will identify the differences in approach between the two countries, and discuss the ways in which the two countries are reliant on or diverging from each other.
84-630.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

84-658.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

99-386.name: Global Issues and AI: Cities and Communities
99-386.desc: THIS COURSE IS A WEEKEND MICRO-COURSE: Oct 23-25, 2026 "Global Issues and AI" critically investigates the paradoxical impact of artificial intelligence on the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Through the lenses of health, labor, urbanization, and climate, students analyze the tension between AI's potential to accelerate or hinder global progress. The course explores the promises and pitfalls of emerging technologies to bridge the divide between the Global North and South.  Future semester stackable micro-courses will include:  Spring 2027- Global Issues and AI: Climate Action  Fall 2027- Global Issues and AI: Health and Well-being  Spring 2028- Global Issues and AI: Work and Economic Growth

99-403.name: Interdisciplinary Leadership Development Seminar
99-403.desc: The seminar is predicated on the six-pillar leadership model of the Center for Leadership Studies, built on the foundation that effective leaders must at once visionary, ethical, engaging, tactical technical (including sub-expert conversancy for team development), and reflective (including formal assessment and redirection, as well the core competencies of a reflective practitioner. The components of the experience include assigned media of 120’, including note taking, delivered via written, video and audio (podcast) media.  The first of two meeting days each week (T/R) will include focused discussion and elucidation of the topic of the week, buttressed by these assigned media.  The second of two meeting days per week will include special guests, case studies, role plays, and other experiential opportunities to deepen student understanding and to practice their underlying leadership skillset.  (The special guests are CEO’s, leaders and influencers in a variety of for-profit and non-profit organizations, reflective of the disciplines reflected in the course composition.)  Each week will also include two hours of “experiential opportunities” (EO’s) to allow students to tailor experience to their own personal and professional ambitions.  (These include joint experiential opportunities spanning all sections facilitated centrally, as well as individual one:one sessions with the Executive Fellows leading each seminar.)  Lastly, each week culminates with a 2-hour (1,200 word +/-) reflective journal that is submitted for detailed Executive Fellow feedback, allowing each student to document and exposit on their own leadership progression.  Requires faculty approval - contact Michael Murphy at mm1v@andrew.cmu.edu

99-786.name: Global Issues and AI: Cities and Communities
99-786.desc: THIS COURSE IS A WEEKEND MICRO-COURSE: Oct 23-25, 2026 "Global Issues and AI" critically investigates the paradoxical impact of artificial intelligence on the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Through the lenses of health, labor, urbanization, and climate, students analyze the tension between AI's potential to accelerate or hinder global progress. The course explores the promises and pitfalls of emerging technologies to bridge the divide between the Global North and South.  Future semester stackable micro-courses will include:  Spring 2027- Global Issues and AI: Climate Action  Fall 2027- Global Issues and AI: Health and Well-being  Spring 2028- Global Issues and AI: Work and Economic Growth

06-324.name: Computational Optimization and Machine Learning for Chemical Engineering
06-324.desc: This course will focus on the development and use of numerical methods and machine learning approaches for chemical engineering. This includes solution of nonlinear equations, differential equations, and constrained optimization problems. The course will also address regression for data science and machine learning. Students will learn how to apply modern machine learning approaches (e.g., neural networks) in the context of engineering problems.

06-763.name: Systems and Toolchains for AI Engineers
06-763.desc: Adopting Artificial Intelligence in modern era has much more to it than learning the theoretical foundation of AI algorithms. The implementation of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence at large scale requires solid technical infrastructure to support its complex, heavy processes. In this course, students will learn to be effective users of AI systems. Students will gain hands-on experience with modern ML frameworks and infrastructure tools, in the context of large real-world datasets and under conditions requiring engineering design choices. This experience will be gained in conjunction with practical application of class topics in a real cloud environment. The premise of this course is to build a broad and solid foundation in Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure that will pay significant dividends throughout a student's research and work career across data science and Artificial Intelligence related fields. In this class, we will focus on the following topics: Data Collection and Storage; Data Streaming; Data Engineering; Modern ML Frameworks; Model Validation and Monitoring; Neural Network Design and Implementation; Embedded Machine Learning; Deployment of ML Models to the Cloud. The course material will focus on recent and landmark research papers and existing tools and software systems. Students will have substantial programming project work in which they design, implement, and analyze aspects of AI-model infrastructure. This course will use an IoT-relevant dataset throughout the semester. The format of this course will be a mix of lectures and hands-on labs. Students will be responsible for readings, and completing a hands-on project focused on developing applications on Apache Spark, TensorFlow, Apache Kafka, and PostgreSQL. Readings will be selected from recent conference proceedings and journals.

09-702.name: Statistical Mechanics and Dynamics
09-702.desc: This course will address the application of statistical mechanics to chemical systems.  Topics to be discussed include the calculation of thermodynamic functions, phase transitions and chemical equilibrium, calculation of the transport properties of gases and liquids and the elementary theory of chemical kinetics.

09-825.name: Special Topics: Mass Spectrometry
09-825.desc: This course covers fundamentals and applications of mass spectrometry applied to solve environmental problems. Applications include detection, identification, and quantification of anthropogenic contaminants in environmental and biological samples including air, water, soil, sediment, and tissue, and characterization of complex natural mixtures such as dissolved organic matter (DOM). We will cover sample preparation concepts, separation techniques, and instrumentation spanning from traditional detectors to new developments, with an emphasis on understanding capabilities and limitations of a range of techniques. Case studies will offer opportunities to analyze and interpret real data to solve environmental problems.

15-474.name: Neural Graphics
15-474.desc: This course explores the rapidly evolving intersection of machine learning and computer graphics, offering a modern perspective on topics traditionally covered in 15- 362. Students will learn how neural methods are transforming the way we represent, render, and animate visual content. Through a combination of lectures, seminar-style discussions, and research-based projects, the course examines how machine learning techniques can accelerate and enhance traditional graphics pipelines. Topics include Neural Texture Compression, Computer Shaders, Neural Shading, Neural Denoising, Gaussian Splatting, Neural Radiance Fields, Inverse Rendering, AI Players, Animation Cycles, Neural Frame Interpolation, & Stylized Animation.

15-674.name: Neural Graphics
15-674.desc: This course explores the rapidly evolving intersection of machine learning and computer graphics, offering a modern perspective on topics traditionally covered in 15- 362. Students will learn how neural methods are transforming the way we represent, render, and animate visual content. Through a combination of lectures, seminar-style discussions, and research-based projects, the course examines how machine learning techniques can accelerate and enhance traditional graphics pipelines. Topics include Neural Texture Compression, Computer Shaders, Neural Shading, Neural Denoising, Gaussian Splatting, Neural Radiance Fields, Inverse Rendering, AI Players, Animation Cycles, Neural Frame Interpolation, & Stylized Animation.

51-209.name: The Business of Design
51-209.desc: This course addresses a critical but often missing component of design education: preparing designers for the real-world business dynamics that shape successful careers after graduation. For students who are serious about building meaningful, sustainable careers—or one day leading their own studios—understanding how design operates within the realities of clients, budgets, expectations, market cycles, macroeconomic forces, and relationships is essential. The course also examines why some designers and studios build lasting success while others struggle to sustain momentum, translating industry lessons into practical guidance for young professionals.  At its core, design is a business of relationships. This course focuses on client development and management, aligning and exceeding expectations, pricing and value creation, negotiation, communication, and professional positioning. Students explore how trust, perception, and experience shape opportunity—how the client’s perception of the work and the collaboration ultimately defines success. Emphasis is placed on the reality that designers work in service of client goals and outcomes, not in isolation of personal taste.  Beyond craft, the course prepares students to think like creative leaders and future founders—learning to work on a business, not just in it. Through real-world case studies, scenarios, and practical examples drawn from professional practice, students gain knowledge rarely taught in design school but essential to building a resilient and rewarding career that can adapt to market cycles, economic shifts, and the evolving realities of the design industry.

51-448.name: Design Fusion: Design Anthropology
51-448.desc: This course explores design anthropology as a cultural, social, and political practice situated at the intersection of understanding and intervention. In moments of increasing complexity, it introduces anthropological approaches for examining how design participates in culture and produces meaning, while also using design methods to better understand how people live and relate. Through work navigating both theory and practice, students move from close attention to everyday objects, to broader systems and social forces, and finally to reflection on their own design assumptions and practices. Emphasizing design as a practice of sense-making, the course encourages students to engage design with greater empathy, care, and responsibility.

51-449.name: Boring Words & Interesting Graphics
51-449.desc: This is an experimental typography course. Students will work on a range of projects, big and small, that will focus on playful interpretation of messages through conceptual typographic expression. We will use typography to make a statement, make typography that contradicts what it states, and make typefaces that communicate without words.

51-455.name: Values-Based Design
51-455.desc: How might a values-based design approach guide innovation for individuals, organizations, and societies? In the "Introduction to Values-Based Design" course, students learn to find new opportunities for innovation around organizational and societal transitions. This course helps students to find innovation opportunities through values alignment innovation process. It is an applied course in which students learn to use values, shared purpose, and desired outcomes to design products, services, and systems that accelerate transition pathways towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and beyond.On the CMU-Q website, it states: "Sustainability is a core value of Carnegie Mellon University, and the Qatar campus embraces this value wholeheartedly. Our community is comprised of faculty, staff, and students, and together we are on a mission to work the UN Sustainability Development Goals (SDGs) into every aspect of campus life."

51-541.name: Design Fusion: Virtual Worldbuilding
51-541.desc: Using concept art techniques and symbolic design, this class explores the world through the lens of the self. Uncover a world within your own mind and learn to listen to the small details that affect your design decisions. Students will learn how to consciously pull from their personal life experiences, passions, and emotional landscape to create designs that are truly unique to them. Processes covered in this class include mindful ideation practices through sketching and iteration. No prior drawing knowledge or concept art skills needed.  This course is taught by Ashley Kenawell.  Ashley is a digital artist and educator with a background in board game and illustration and concept art.  Her speciality is creating worlds and stories that reflect parts of the inner-self and teaching others to communicate their own self exploration through character and environment design.

66-507.name: Capstone for Environmental and Sustainability Studies
66-507.desc: This undergraduate research course is designed to give students a venue to develop skills for interdisciplinary research in Environmental and Sustainability Studies. The purpose of this undergraduate research capstone is to: 1) Create a sense of community for students pursuing research in interdisciplinary Environmental and Sustainability Studies. 2) Provide guidance for student research projects in interdisciplinary Environmental and Sustainability Studies.   As part of this course, students will set, define, and meet milestones for an undergraduate-level interdisciplinary research project in Environmental and Sustainability Studies. By meeting and presenting milestones and end-of-session products to peers and faculty, students will understand more about their own disciplinary and interdisciplinary engagements with Environmental and Sustainability Studies, and also learn to articulate their unique strengths in an interdisciplinary group setting.

54-215.name: Theater History I: 500 BCE-1640
54-215.desc: OPEN TO NON-MAJORS: Theatre History 500 BCE to 1640 is the first in a three-part world theatre history sequence designed to explore the development of dramatic forms, theatre practices, and performances from the 5th century BCE to today. World Theatre 500 BCE to 1640 investigates histories of theatre and performance (scripts, embodiment, design, audiences, conventions, cultural functions, etc.) within local and global social, artistic and political contexts. The course focuses on evidence and interpretation as well as historical causation. Within each survey section, we will analyze and compare representative case studies to better understand performance as a practice and as a site of history making, with particular attention to questions of race, gender, sexuality, and class. Throughout the semester, we will explore a variety of theatre and performance forms, including Roman comedy, early Sanskrit drama, medieval commemorative drama, and Japanese theatre forms including Noh and Kabuki, among others. We will investigate world theatre history from a historiographical perspective. This means that we will examine our material not only for content, but also for how it conveys that content. In our exploration of how theatre history is crafted, we will develop critical historical skills and tools, including how to ask historical questions, assess primary sources, critique narratives, and clearly communicate our historiographical ideas and arguments. Students will produce historical knowledge about theatre and performance with respect to questions of racial, gender, sexual, and class diversity throughout the semester.

54-387.name: Choreography & Composition
54-387.desc: This course introduces the principles, language, and technique in the art of choreography and composition as applicable to all areas of study in the School of Drama, including Acting/MT, Directing, Dramaturgy, Production Management, Dramatic Writing, Scenic, Media, Costume, Lighting, and Sound Design.  This year-long course is organized into two semesters involving lectures, discussion, and project-based styles of engagement.     Students will create a progressive series of assignments and studies in collaboration, improvisation, building a phrase, theme and variation, retrograde, deconstruction, abstraction, vocabulary, history, professional language, and dance vocabulary which culminate in studio presentations,  dance on film, and site-specific work.

54-572.name: Costume Crafts: Leather Explorations
54-572.desc: This course will explore the many ways that real leather is used in the realm of costume crafts.  We will examine footwear, sword belts, armor and masks.  We will deal with proper coloring, decoration, stitching and finishing techniques.  Students will leave empowered with vocabulary, basic skills and project work exploring a variety of leather types and manipulation techniques.

54-734.name: Introduction to AutoCAD 2D
54-734.desc: An introduction to 2D drafting in AutoCAD, primarily in a theatre technology environment.

54-735.name: Text to Stage II: Global Theatre Traditions
54-735.desc: What different forms of theatre have evolved? What is theatre's function? This director seminar investigates these questions by examining seminal international theatre traditions across distinct historical eras. Directors engage comparatively with each tradition, identifying dramaturgical structures and performance conventions. We will read and analyze scripts as well as view recorded performances. Traditions studied include Sanskrit Drama, Zaju, Noh, Kabuki, Anti-Apartheid Theatre, Epic Theatre, and Postmodern Drama. The course expands directors' understanding of theatre as a phenomenon, while also potentially fostering creative inspiration. Course projects are a presentation, a practice-based creative project, and an essay.

54-760.name: Foundations of Scenic Design
54-760.desc: This course will introduce students to the principles and methods of designing scenery using the development of ideas based on a text.

54-772.name: Costume Crafts: Leather Exploration
54-772.desc: This course will explore the many ways that real leather is used in the realm of costume crafts.  We will examine footwear, sword belts, armor and masks.  We will deal with proper coloring, decoration, stitching and finishing techniques.  Students will leave empowered with vocabulary, basic skills and project work exploring a variety of leather types and manipulation techniques.

19-655.name: Special Topics: New Technology Development and Roadmapping
19-655.desc: This course teaches a set of quantitative analysis methods fundamental to technology development and assessing the potential of emerging technologies. Students apply the analysis methods to a particular technology of their choosing in a project. The analysis tools learned in the course allow students to identify critical factors for advancing emerging technologies, strategizing R&D to meet technical and market adoption targets, and predicting future technology performance. Topics include production models, adoption S-curves, dynamic consumer preferences, materials selection, and valuation of technological breakthroughs. Assignments include a series of presentations and written reports. The course assumes familiarity with college-level introductory probability and statistics.

19-746.name: Special Topics: Fundamentals of Responsible AI
19-746.desc: This course provides an interdisciplinary introduction to the key principles and topics in responsible AI, including bias, fairness, interpretability, explainability, privacy, robustness, and safety. Students will develop an understanding of these topics from multiple stakeholder perspectives. The course will cover key methods in responsible AI, drawing on machine learning, statistics, and economics. It will also examine emerging frameworks in AI policy and regulation.

76-322.name: Arranged Marriage
76-322.desc: Arranged marriage has become an object of fascination in a contemporary context of globalization—a point of outrage, curiosity, and even envy. Some renounce arranged marriage as an oppressive, outdated custom, while others reinvigorate the practice in new forms, and for new reasons. Using a series of site-based texts, this course explores representations of arranged marriage (both positive and negative) and the institution itself across global cultural contexts. We will look at the shift in definitions of "force" in annulment cases in the UK by brought by both male and female petitioners. We will examine the romanticisation of arranged marriages in films and television programs. We will consider the economic and social forces that give rise to transnational arranged marriages. Finally, we will explore new methods of arrangement in a period of social media, the rise of the "arranged love marriage," and new traditions.

76-334.name: Pitching to the Business of Entertainment
76-334.desc: The entertainment industry is a dynamic ecosystem where creativity and business intersect. Pitching to the Business of Entertainment introduces students to the process of developing, packaging, and presenting creative projects as viable business opportunities. The course explores how ideas move from concept to market by examining key areas such as intellectual property, development, financing strategies, production planning, distribution pathways, and marketing.  Throughout the semester, students will develop an original film, series or new media project and learn how to communicate its creative and commercial value through professional pitch materials. A central component of the course is the creation of both a Creative Pitch Deck and a Business Pitch Deck, designed to present the project's story, visual approach, target audience, revenue model, and market positioning.  A significant portion of the course is dedicated to the production of a professional trailer that supports the pitch. Students will plan, shoot, and edit a short trailer that conveys the tone, world, and core idea of their project, using it as a visual proof-of-concept for potential investors, producers, and distributors. The course concludes with a formal pitch presentation to an industry-style panel, where students present their decks and trailer and respond to questions. Emphasis is placed on clear communication, persuasive storytelling, and the ability to position creative work within the realities of the entertainment marketplace.

76-366.name: Grant and Proposal Writing
76-366.desc: How do writers persuade organizations to fund ideas, support academic research, approve projects, or adopt proposed solutions? This course examines how proposals function in nonprofit organizations, academic research settings, public agencies, and business environments. Students analyze real proposals to understand audience expectations, evaluation criteria, and funding guidelines, then develop their own proposals tailored to specific opportunities and organizational contexts. Students will produce grant applications, academic research proposals, organizational analyses, business proposals, or other funding and approval documents aligned with their disciplinary or professional interests. Coursework emphasizes defining problems, articulating measurable goals, presenting evidence, and justifying budgets and timelines in clear, compelling language. For Professional and Technical Writing majors, the course strengthens advanced persuasive writing, strategic document design, and client-centered communication skills; for students in other disciplines, it provides practical experience developing research proposals, seeking funding, and advocating for projects in academic, nonprofit, corporate, or public-sector environments.

76-375.name: Emerging Technologies in Writing
76-375.desc: Emerging Technologies in Writing examines how new and evolving technologies such as generative AI, personalized content including SEO, augmented and virtual reality, data-driven composing, microcontent writing, and writing for conversational agents, are reshaping rhetorical practice. Students will explore how these technologies influence authorship, collaboration, agency, genre, audience engagement, and the role of human-machine collaboration in writing. Combining critical theory, hands-on experimentation, and design-oriented projects, the course will equip students with the technical, analytical, ethical, and creative competencies needed to write with, through, and about emerging technologies. Throughout the semester, students will engage in rhetorical analysis, multimodal composition, tool critique, and informed decision-making to understand how writing is evolving and how communicators can shape responsible technological futures.

76-381.name: AI Filmmaking and Creative Arts Lab
76-381.desc: This course introduces students to the intersection of artificial intelligence and creative storytelling, equipping them with the tools and critical thinking skills to navigate emerging production workflows in visual media.   Students explore how AI can enhance narrative development and production processes while preserving the human creativity at the center of filmmaking. Through hands on experimentation, students work with commercially available AI tools that are transforming the media landscape, including scriptwriting, image generation, storyboarding, video creation, animation, visual effects, and postproduction. These tools are used as part of a complete narrative pipeline that leads to the development of an original short film and reaserch.   A central component of the course is the AI Film Lab (locaed at Posner Hall 261), a dedicated studio environment where students experiment with AI driven workflows in a practical setting. The lab includes immersive Dolby Atmos sound, editing suites, motion capture capabilities, and flexible filming space where generative media can interact with physical performance and traditional filmmaking techniques. Graduate students from different disciplines are encouraged to integrate AI tools into their existing creative practice, whether in art, drama, technical production, or media related fields.  By the end of the course, students complete an AI assisted narrative short film and gain practical experience with the tools, workflows, and critical frameworks shaping the next generation of filmmaking.
