Students analyze both the creative possibilities and the ethical and legal implications of AI in visual media, developing a critical perspective on how these technologies influence authorship, creative practice, and the future of the entertainment industry.

76-455.name: The Pittsburgh Review of Books (PRoB)
76-455.desc: The Pittsburgh Review of Books, an interdisciplinary public humanities publication that publishes engaged, incisive, and smart cultural criticism and analysis for an educated and non-specialist audience is looking for students who will work as staff writers. In this course, students will learn about freelance writing, editing, and publishing while gaining real-world, hands-on experience with a publication housed in the English Department that has featured Pulitzer nominees, Guggenheim Fellows, and first-time writers. In addition to the practical work of helping to run a national publication, students will also learn about the burgeoning movement, discipline, and methodology of public humanities, becoming familiar with the publishing ecosystem and the variety of sites and authors who work within this environment. The first semester will be focused on the writing of long-form narrative journalism while the second semester examines trade book publishing. Students are free to enroll in either or both of those courses.

76-734.name: Pitching to the Business of Entertainment
76-734.desc: The entertainment industry is a dynamic ecosystem where creativity and business intersect. Pitching to the Business of Entertainment introduces students to the process of developing, packaging, and presenting creative projects as viable business opportunities. The course explores how ideas move from concept to market by examining key areas such as intellectual property, development, financing strategies, production planning, distribution pathways, and marketing.  Throughout the semester, students will develop an original film, series or new media project and learn how to communicate its creative and commercial value through professional pitch materials. A central component of the course is the creation of both a Creative Pitch Deck and a Business Pitch Deck, designed to present the project's story, visual approach, target audience, revenue model, and market positioning.  A significant portion of the course is dedicated to the production of a professional trailer that supports the pitch. Students will plan, shoot, and edit a short trailer that conveys the tone, world, and core idea of their project, using it as a visual proof-of-concept for potential investors, producers, and distributors. The course concludes with a formal pitch presentation to an industry-style panel, where students present their decks and trailer and respond to questions. Emphasis is placed on clear communication, persuasive storytelling, and the ability to position creative work within the realities of the entertainment marketplace.

76-766.name: Grant and Proposal Writing
76-766.desc: How do writers persuade organizations to fund ideas, support academic research, approve projects, or adopt proposed solutions? This course examines how proposals function in nonprofit organizations, academic research settings, public agencies, and business environments. Students analyze real proposals to understand audience expectations, evaluation criteria, and funding guidelines, then develop their own proposals tailored to specific opportunities and organizational contexts. Students will produce grant applications, academic research proposals, organizational analyses, business proposals, or other funding and approval documents aligned with their disciplinary or professional interests. Coursework emphasizes defining problems, articulating measurable goals, presenting evidence, and justifying budgets and timelines in clear, compelling language. For Professional and Technical Writing majors, the course strengthens advanced persuasive writing, strategic document design, and client-centered communication skills; for students in other disciplines, it provides practical experience developing research proposals, seeking funding, and advocating for projects in academic, nonprofit, corporate, or public-sector environments.

76-775.name: Emerging Technologies in Writing
76-775.desc: Emerging Technologies in Writing examines how new and evolving technologies such as generative AI, personalized content including SEO, augmented and virtual reality, data-driven composing, microcontent writing, and writing for conversational agents, are reshaping rhetorical practice. Students will explore how these technologies influence authorship, collaboration, agency, genre, audience engagement, and the role of human-machine collaboration in writing. Combining critical theory, hands-on experimentation, and design-oriented projects, the course will equip students with the technical, analytical, ethical, and creative competencies needed to write with, through, and about emerging technologies. Throughout the semester, students will engage in rhetorical analysis, multimodal composition, tool critique, and informed decision-making to understand how writing is evolving and how communicators can shape responsible technological futures.

76-781.name: AI Filmmaking and Creative Arts Lab
76-781.desc: This course introduces students to the intersection of artificial intelligence and creative storytelling, equipping them with the tools and critical thinking skills to navigate emerging production workflows in visual media.   Students explore how AI can enhance narrative development and production processes while preserving the human creativity at the center of filmmaking. Through hands on experimentation, students work with commercially available AI tools that are transforming the media landscape, including scriptwriting, image generation, storyboarding, video creation, animation, visual effects, and postproduction. These tools are used as part of a complete narrative pipeline that leads to the development of an original short film and reaserch.   A central component of the course is the AI Film Lab (locaed at Posner Hall 261), a dedicated studio environment where students experiment with AI driven workflows in a practical setting. The lab includes immersive Dolby Atmos sound, editing suites, motion capture capabilities, and flexible filming space where generative media can interact with physical performance and traditional filmmaking techniques. Graduate students from different disciplines are encouraged to integrate AI tools into their existing creative practice, whether in art, drama, technical production, or media related fields.  By the end of the course, students complete an AI assisted narrative short film and gain practical experience with the tools, workflows, and critical frameworks shaping the next generation of filmmaking. Students analyze both the creative possibilities and the ethical and legal implications of AI in visual media, developing a critical perspective on how these technologies influence authorship, creative practice, and the future of the entertainment industry.

76-786.name: Language and Culture
76-786.desc: This course is an introduction into the scholarship surrounding the nature of language and the question of how language shapes and is shaped by social, cultural and political contexts. We will begin by studying important literature in linguistics and language theory, both to introduce us to how scholars think about language and to give us a shared vocabulary to use for the rest of the semester. We will then move into case studies and theoretical works exploring the intersections of language use, individual and group identities, and the exercise of power, in its many forms. In particular, we will focus on the relationship between language and culture by asking, in what ways does language influence and constitute social change? How is social change reflected by changes in the way we use language? Over the course of the semester, you will work on applying the knowledge and theoretical tools you gain to your own analysis of a linguistic artifact that you choose.

76-855.name: The Pittsburgh Review of Books (PRoB)
76-855.desc: The Pittsburgh Review of Books, an interdisciplinary public humanities publication that publishes engaged, incisive, and smart cultural criticism and analysis for an educated and non-specialist audience is looking for students who will work as staff writers. In this course, students will learn about freelance writing, editing, and publishing while gaining real-world, hands-on experience with a publication housed in the English Department that has featured Pulitzer nominees, Guggenheim Fellows, and first-time writers. In addition to the practical work of helping to run a national publication, students will also learn about the burgeoning movement, discipline, and methodology of public humanities, becoming familiar with the publishing ecosystem and the variety of sites and authors who work within this environment. The first semester will be focused on the writing of long-form narrative journalism while the second semester examines trade book publishing. Students are free to enroll in either or both of those courses.

53-772.name: Modern Making - How to Make (Almost) Anything
53-772.desc: Have you ever wanted to bring your digital ideas into the physical world—to make something you can touch, press, or wear? Have you ever wanted to make your own robot, musical instrument, or motion-sensing art piece—but you weren't sure where to begin? Soldering, 3D printing, AI, laser-cutting, microcontrollers, and more: these are the foundational tools and techniques used to prototype interactive physical systems. Combining physical fabrication, electronics, and some modern AI tools, this hands-on prototyping course will teach all the core skills needed to build an MVP of (almost) anything. Students will learn how to design, fabricate, and assemble custom hardware while developing an understanding of inputs, outputs, and embedded control. The course also introduces contemporary prototyping workflows, including the use of AI-assisted coding and design tools to accelerate development. By the end of the course, students will propose and build an interactive system that bridges the digital and physical worlds.

94-862.name: Global Issues and AI: Cities and Communities
94-862.desc: THIS COURSE IS A WEEKEND MICRO-COURSE: Oct 23-25, 2026 "Global Issues and AI" critically investigates the paradoxical impact of artificial intelligence on the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Through the lenses of health, labor, urbanization, and climate, students analyze the tension between AI's potential to accelerate or hinder global progress. The course explores the promises and pitfalls of emerging technologies to bridge the divide between the Global North and South. Future semester stackable micro-courses will include: Spring 2027- Global Issues and AI: Climate Action Fall 2027- Global Issues and AI: Health and Well-being Spring 2028- Global Issues and AI: Work and Economic Growth

94-868.name: GeoAI: Advanced GIS for Policy and Design
94-868.desc: As cities confront climate risk and social inequity, effective policy relies on advanced spatial intelligence. This course introduces GeoAI, the integration of GIS and AI, as a framework to empower decision makers with evidence-based insights. Students will analyze satellite imagery and socioeconomic spatial data to tackle challenges, such as heat vulnerability and environmental justice. Using ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online, students will perform raster analysis, predictive modeling, and deep learning classification. Beyond technical implementation, the course focuses on how to make informed decisions by assessing bias and uncertainty. No prior coding is required; the focus remains on making complex GeoAI workflows accessible for urban planning and policy. Through hands-on activities, students will learn to communicate findings through policy-oriented maps, culminating in a final project that designs a reproducible GeoAI workflow to support real-world policy interventions and empower leadership with the tools needed to address growing urban inequities.

79-166.name: Women and the World: Beyond the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1914-2016
79-166.desc: When the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on December 10, 1948, it marked a new era in international relations and a new standard of global citizenship. This course focuses on the intense drafting and adoption process for the document, the decades of fighting, lobbying, and negotiations that preceded it, and the successes and disappointments that accompanied the declaration and similar UN proclamations. In particular, this course centers women's roles in this process. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt, as Chair of the Commission on Human Rights which drafted the Declaration, will obviously be a main character. But students will also learn about the other women who took center stage during the eventful and dynamic interwar years and beyond - Black internationalists, nurses and Red Cross coordinators, peace activists from around the globe, and isolationists who opposed the very idea of the UN. These women populated a constellation of actors who promoted and contested the construction of institutions for world governance. To understand this process, we will trace the creation of internationalist and isolationist foreign policy circles; and examine the consequences of the many crises of the interwar period on the actors who comprised such circles. By studying the creation and maintenance of the United Nations and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, students will learn how ideas of world government, citizenship, and diplomacy have dominated and been challenged in American life, implicating a host of sectors, including education, public policy, law, racial justice, and international relations.

79-167.name: Archaeology of Violence
79-167.desc: This course, "Archaeology of Violence," introduces students to archaeological and anthropological methods used to investigate violence in past and recent human societies. The course examines how material remains like human skeletal evidence, burial contexts, and landscapes can reveal patterns of conflict, structural inequality, and mass atrocity. Particular attention is given to humanitarian and forensic contexts, including mass grave investigation, human rights documentation, and post-conflict recovery efforts. Students will learn how archaeologists and anthropologists collaborate to document violence, identify the dead, and syncretize technological methods with local ideals of justice and memorialization.

79-394.name: Exploring History through Geography
79-394.desc: For studying the past, space can be as important as time. Digital mapping and GeoLocation technologies influence our everyday interactions and perceptions of the world around us. Historians are thinking about how these technologies can change their fields of study, too.  Through the "spatial turn" in the Humanities and Social Sciences, historians are using spatial experience to think more deeply about the meaning of place and space. Visualizing spatial relationships via new technologies can offer meaningful new ways to approach historical questions. This course will consider viewpoints from the discipline of Geography and explore the impact of new methods in the Digital Humanities, including the impact of digital tools such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS).

79-724.name: Social Movements
79-724.desc: In this seminar, we will examine the methodological, theoretical, and ethical questions that historians face when studying social movements. How have historians approached social movements and what sources have they relied on to understand them? How have historians of social movements grappled with theories of social change? While we will explore these questions across distinct time periods and national boundaries, this is not a comprehensive survey of social movements. Rather, we will focus on time periods, regions, and social movements that are of particular interest to each of us in the course. Our goal will be to learn from how historians have studied social movements, and to apply these lessons to our own research and writing.

05-312.name: The AI Augmented Designer
05-312.desc: The AI Augmented Designer satisfies one design studio requirement course within the HCII and explores how designers can augment and accelerate their work with the use of AI. The course involves explorations of AI use across the design process. Students design and develop four prototypes on their own. They document their process and critically reflect on if and how AI changes their practice for better or worse. The course helps students develop an understanding of when and where AI can best support their work. Throughout the course, we have readings and discussions on scholarly thought regarding the symbiosis of designers and AI.  This course is intended for students with strong design fundamentals looking to take the next step in their work. The course introduces students to off-the-shelf tools as well as skills for building their own augmentation tools using generally available AI systems.

05-416.name: Applied Research Methods
05-416.desc: This course provides a foundation in basic research methods while maintaining a strong applied focus on real-world problems. This course is for advanced undergraduate students (juniors  and seniors) interested in participating in research projects in the future (e.g., independent studies) and graduate students who will carry out behavioral research in the context of technology (e.g., social effects of technology, evaluation of technology, robots and agents, use of sensors to predict user behavior). The course will be run as a combination of discussion seminars and labs involving hands-on practice of skills such as experimentation, survey design, observation, interviews, and data analyses. Students will complete a research project in the course.

05-612.name: The AI Augmented Designer
05-612.desc: The AI Augmented Designer satisfies one design studio requirement course within the HCII and explores how designers can augment and accelerate their work with the use of AI. The course involves explorations of AI use across the design process. Students design and develop four prototypes on their own. They document their process and critically reflect on if and how AI changes their practice for better or worse. The course helps students develop an understanding of when and where AI can best support their work. Throughout the course, we have readings and discussions on scholarly thought regarding the symbiosis of designers and AI.  This course is intended for students with strong design fundamentals looking to take the next step in their work. The course introduces students to off-the-shelf tools as well as skills for building their own augmentation tools using generally available AI systems.

67-290.name: Storytelling with Data Visualization
67-290.desc: The course complements existing offerings by providing students with a high-impact, design-oriented experience that emphasizes visual perception, storytelling techniques, and the critical evaluation of information, skills essential in modern data-driven fields. Specifically: * Business students will deepen their ability to communicate insights to stakeholders. * IS and CS students will connect visualization theory to software design and user experience. * Biological sciences students will learn to visualize complex scientific data for reports, posters, and publications. This micro course broadens CMU-Q's curriculum in a way that is both practically relevant and academically enriching.

67-342.name: Data Governance in the Age of AI
67-342.desc: This course provides a comprehensive foundation in data governance principles, frameworks, and organizational implementation strategies, with an emphasis on the evolving regulatory and ethical landscape shaped by artificial intelligence. Students will develop practical skills in designing governance operating models, ensuring compliance with regulatory frameworks, and managing the intersection of traditional data governance with emerging AI governance challenges. The goal of this course is to prepare students to lead data and AI governance initiatives in real-world organizational settings.

67-347.name: AI for an Inclusive Digital Experience
67-347.desc: This course explores the transformative power of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create a more inclusive digital landscape. Students will examine how AI systems can be intentionally designed to be accessible, fair, and beneficial for individuals across a diverse spectrum of abilities. The course begins by mapping the digital divide, analyzing how technology has historically reinforced or bridged inequalities based on gender, socioeconomic status, and disability. Students then delve into a core methodology for designing inclusive AI interfaces through five critical pillars: Interactivity, Adaptability, Context Awareness, Predictive Assistance, and Learning & Improvement. During the semester, students will: • Apply Human-Centered Design: Utilize frameworks like the Jordan's Pleasure Model to prioritize inclusion from the initial design phase.  • Innovate for Diverse Needs: Explore AI solutions specifically tailored for visual, hearing, motor, and cognitive disabilities.  • Mitigate Algorithmic Bias: Examine how incomplete or biased training data can lead to exclusion and learn strategies to ensure representational fairness.  • Analyze Policy and Ethics: Address the long-term ethical implications of AI and advocate for disability-centric legislative agendas.  By the end of the course, students will possess the skills to design AI systems that are technically robust, ethically grounded, and universally accessible. These skills are put into practice through a semester-long capstone project, where students design a real-world AI experience that addresses common inclusion challenges.

67-736.name: Building Data Visualizations in to Information Systems
67-736.desc: In an increasingly data-driven world, the ability to effectively understand complex information is crucial for problem-solving and decision-making. This course explores the art and science of designing interactive visualizations within information systems to allow data to be effectively communicated and understood.  In other words, to allow the user to more easily and fully grasp the underlying story.  Students in this course will gain a comprehensive understanding of the principles and theories underlying information design and visualization, including topics related to information architecture, human computer interaction, user-centered design, human perceptual and cognitive factors and how to leverage them to effectively communicate information. Students will also learn how these visualizations can be integrated into the software design process and how visualizations improve the value of information systems. Through a well-balanced breadth and depth of lectures, exercises and projects, students will learn to use popular design tools and technologies to design information systems and create visualizations that facilitate understanding, analysis, assessment and evaluation of various data sets and selected information systems.  One of the important aspects of this course is to foster students' cultural and socioeconomic awareness, promote responsible technology use, and empower them to apply technical skills to address social inequalities for positive societal impact.

67-742.name: Data Governance in the Age of AI
67-742.desc: Data Governance in the Age of AI

67-747.name: AI for an Inclusive Digital Experience
67-747.desc: AI for an Inclusive Digital Experience

67-748.name: Black Mirror - Cultural Representations of Technology
67-748.desc: Advances in technology raise a variety of fascinating ethical, cultural, and societal questions often resulting in uncertainties and unanticipated dilemmas. This course provides an  opportunity to explore how cultural representations of technology are reflected in society  and inform continued technical advancements. Using episodes from Black Mirror - a British  anthology television series created by Charlie Brooker - we will explore the depictions of  technology and society and its representation.  This course will challenge you to think critically about technological change and  controversial topics surrounding digital culture and social impact. You will also develop a  more sophisticated understanding of the political, economic, and cultural considerations that underlie technological development. Discussions of episodes will be supplemented by  popular, critical texts and academic articles. This class is more seminar-based, rather than  lecture-based. We will engage critically and constructively in key debates that shape the  future of the technology, through in-class discussions, activities, and presentations.

67-768.name: User Experience (UX) Research for Product Managers
67-768.desc: User Experience (UX) saturates the digital landscape, often acting as the pivotal determinant of user engagement with a product or service. Mastery of UX research is crucial for product managers, serving as the cornerstone for steering development efforts towards the attainment of cutting-edge user experiences. This course is geared towards providing understanding of the pivotal role of UX within the realm of product management, equipping students with the requisite arsenal of tools to research, obtain, and leverage UX insights for the development of products. The curriculum introduces UX principles, and delves in UX research methodologies, and their practical application through advanced digital experimentation. Through participation in hands-on exercises within a state-of-the-art digital laboratory environment, participants will go on the iterative journey from problem identification to the delivery of definitive solutions, thereby fine-tuning their acumen in elevating UX across the product lifecycle. By integrating theoretical paradigms with experiential learning, this course empowers participants to deftly navigate the intricacies of UX research, catalyzing the creation of next-generation, user-centric digital innovations.

95-856.name: Securing and Scaling AI Infrastructure
95-856.desc: Scaling Artificial Intelligence workloads require high-performance networking, storage, and compute systems differnet than traditional enterprise workflows. As the need for AI across industries are accelerating, traditional network infrastructure cannot scale. The course dives into how to scale and secure AI infrastructure, focusing on network topologies, storage, and compute clusters that are used today. Students will research and write about current challenges industries are facing as part of the course.

95-877.name: Strategic Communication for Information Systems Leaders

95-896.name: Python for Software Development
95-896.desc: This course focuses on the fundamentals of computer programming using the Python programming language. Students will develop their problem-solving skills using the top-down procedural decomposition and object-oriented design to build real-world based software applications. Students will also learn to use common Python libraries for data analysis and plotting. Assignments will include weekly homework and fundamental checkpoint quizzes, top-down approach programming projects within a group data focused project.  Learners will study how to build professional, user-friendly computer programs applicable to real-world applications.

49-420.name: EDIE Innovation Capstone
49-420.desc: In this course, students work in a team-based project, starting from an open-ended problem area and concluding with a refined product/service concept. Methods and skills from prior classes (e.g., innovation process and methods, customer discovery, engineering design) will be applied and practiced by the team. The skills learned in this course can be applied to the for-profit sector and also in the context of projects for social good.

11-752.name: Speech Generation
11-752.desc: This course provides an in-depth study of speech synthesis and generative speech modeling, tracing the evolution from classical signal-processing and statistical approaches to modern neural and foundation-based methods. The course begins with the fundamentals of human speech production, which motivate early synthesis techniques such as concatenative and statistical parametric models, and then progresses to deep learning-based acoustic modeling, neural vocoding, and end-to-end speech generation architectures. Contemporary topics include the integration of large language models with speech synthesis, the use of discrete and continuous speech representations, and emerging paradigms for scalable and controllable speech generation. Beyond text-to-speech, the course covers a broad range of generative speech problems, including voice conversion, expressive speech synthesis, prosody generation and manipulation, speech editing, speech-to-speech translation, and spoken dialogue systems. Additional topics address disentangled representation learning, evaluation methodologies, speech databases, and security considerations such as spoofing attacks.  Days of Week: Monday, Wednesday  Time: 9:30 - 10:50  Enrollment is 30  Will you have a final exam? No, final project  Letter grades or option to Pass/Fail? Letter grades   Best regards,  Carlos  ________________________________  Professor, IEEE Fellow, ISCA Fellow Carnegie Mellon University School of Computer Science  Language Technologies Institute

11-768.name: AI Agents
11-768.desc: "This course focuses on LLM-based AI agents: autonomous systems that use large language models to perceive, reason, plan, and act in complex environments. These systems represent a shift toward multi-step task completion requiring sustained interaction with external environments. LLM agents have already demonstrated a substantial impact on software development through code generation, and are poised to impact other digital domains.  Developing capable agents requires specializing standard LLM training methods, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, to the agentic domains. These systems face unique research challenges such as environmental grounding and long-horizon credit assignment, which provide significant opportunities for technical exploration. This course covers foundational capabilities like instruction following, tool use, memory, and task decomposition alongside practical considerations such as safety sandboxing, credentialing, and the use of modern development frameworks. Students will learn these established foundations as well as explore open research frontiers: advanced search techniques, and interaction with people and other agents.  This course is intended for graduate students. Familiarity with training neural language models is required.

11-904.name: Python for Data Science I
11-904.desc: Students learn the concepts, techniques, skills, and tools needed for developing programs in Python. Core topics include types, variables, functions, iteration, conditionals, data structures, classes, objects, modules, and I/O operations. Students get an introductory experience with several development environments, including Jupyter Notebook, as well as selected software development practices, such as test-driven development, debugging, and style. Course projects include real-life applications on enterprise data and document manipulation, web scraping, and data analysis.

11-905.name: Python for Data Science II
11-905.desc: Students learn the concepts, techniques, skills, and tools needed for developing programs in Python. Core topics include types, variables, functions, iteration, conditionals, data structures, classes, objects, modules, and I/O operations. Students get an introductory experience with several development environments, including Jupyter Notebook, as well as selected software development practices, such as test-driven development, debugging, and style. Course projects include real-life applications on enterprise data and document manipulation, web scraping, and data analysis.

82-116.name: Elementary Arabic 2 Online
82-116.desc: This course is a second-semester Arabic that builds on Elementary Arabic I. It is for learners who have completed a first-semester Arabic or its equivalent and wish to learn Modern Standard Arabic (MSA)اللغة العربية الفصحى / al-luġa al-ʿarabiyya al-fuṣḥā, the language form used for reading, formal writing, and formal speaking (for example, in formal news media, lectures, religious sermons, etc...) and the Egyptian مصري and/or Levantine شامي dialects.  This course continues to introduce students to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) to achieve communicative competence at the Novice-High/Intermediate-Low level in all language skills (listening, speaking, reading, and writing). The course covers five lessons of an interactive online textbook designed for second-semester Arabic. The online textbook contains all necessary audio-visuals, digital narratives, practice exercises, culture, and assessments. No need to purchase any supplementary material. This course follows a flipped-learning design. Students are responsible for preparation of the assigned modules before class, allowing to dedicate class time to active communication and skills-based practice in writing, reading, speaking, and listening.

82-189.name: AI Literacy for Global Cultures: Prompts, Agents, Workflow and Vibe Development
82-189.desc: This course introduces students with no prior technical experience to digital literacies through AI, autonomous agents, automated workflows, and vibe development. Students learn to build with AI as their coding partner, progressing from basic AI literacy to creating autonomous agents and automated workflows. Topics include advanced prompting and prompt engineering, building AI agents that can perform tasks independently, designing and automating multi-step workflows without traditional coding, debugging and iterating on AI-generated code through vibe coding, and creating custom chatbots and information retrieval systems. Students apply these skills by creating projects that engage meaningfully with global cultures, such as multilingual educational tools, interactive cultural archives, community knowledge platforms, and digital preservation projects. The emphasis is on using emerging technology to build tools that preserve cultural traditions, facilitate cross-cultural communication, and celebrate diverse perspectives.

82-364.name: Investigating Italy through Crime Fiction
82-364.desc: The course will examine Italian crime fiction as a counter-narrative to Italian history, culture, and society from the 1930s to the present. Through a selected corpus of crime novels, short stories, films, and TV series, students will be offered an alternative perspective on social issues and themes related to justice and injustice. Class discussions and assignments will include ongoing reflections on the historical events, political changes, and social conditions that give rise to crime, with particular attention to themes such as social class inequality, dysfunctional power dynamics, gender-based violence, migration, environmental injustice, and political corruption in relation to the Italian justice system. Students will analyze and discuss crime stories inspired by, or that can be connected to, sociopolitical events and the cultural climate of their time, examining how Italian society has responded across different historical periods and contexts (e.g., antifascism, political activism, protests, anti-mafia movements). The course will include texts by sociopolitically engaged authors who combine literature, political activism, and the defense of civil rights, such as Leonardo Sciascia—who exposed connections between the state and the mafia in Sicily—and Massimo Carlotto, who spent several years in prison following a miscarriage of justice and has denounced abuses within the penitentiary system as well as large-scale corruption.

82-723.name: Strategies for Academic English
82-723.desc: Through whole-class workshops and individualized consultations, students in this course will strengthen their academic literacy practices across disciplinary situations. Students will learn how to interpret the expectations of new academic genres and make effective rhetorical and pragmatic choices based on audience, purpose, and context. Using texts drawn from their concurrent coursework—such as research articles, proposals, literature reviews, conference presentations, and seminar papers—students will practice analyzing scholarly writing, synthesizing complex sources, and communicating with clarity and professional awareness. Emphasis is placed on transferable strategies that can be applied across evolving academic and professional situations.  By the end of the semester, students will have developed personalized, research-informed strategies that they can adapt to new academic and professional situations.

10-630.name: Master's Thesis Research
10-630.desc: Course for Master of Science in Machine Learning - Advanced Study students to work with their advisor on research.

10-749.name: AI for Scientific Computing
10-749.desc: AI for Scientific Computing introduces emerging techniques at the intersection of AI, machine learning, and applied mathematics for solving computational problems in the sciences. The course is technical in nature and covers the mathematical foundations of these methods, practical engineering details, benchmarking of current approaches, and obstacles to deployment in real-world scientific settings. Topics include physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), PDE solvers and surrogate models such as neural operators, with applications to computational fluid dynamics and climate; discrete and continuous diffusion models, with applications to protein design and nonequilibrium systems; learned samplers for rare-event sampling and chemical engineering; and inverse problems approached with diffusion-model-based techniques. The course emphasizes how modern AI methods can be used to model, accelerate, and solve scientific computing problems across domains such as fluid dynamics, climate, protein design, and chemical engineering.

10-753.name: Deep Learning and GenAI Theory
10-753.desc: This course studies the theoretical foundations of modern deep learning and generative artificial intelligence. While deep neural networks and generative models have achieved remarkable empirical success across many domains, many of the theoretical principles underlying their behavior are still being actively developed. The goal of this course is to provide a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding these methods and analyzing their theoretical properties. The course will cover theoretical perspectives on deep neural networks, including expressivity, approximation theory, optimization landscapes, and generalization in overparameterized models. We will study the role of gradient-based optimization, stochastic dynamics, and convergence properties of large neural networks. We will also examine modern phenomena observed in deep learning systems, such as double descent, implicit regularization, and grokking. A central focus of the course will be the theory of generative models. Topics will include generative adversarial networks, score-based generative models, diffusion models, and flow-based models. We will analyze these models from probabilistic, optimization, and stochastic-process perspectives, connecting them to concepts such as optimal transport, Langevin dynamics, stochastic differential equations, Fokker-Planck equation, Schrödinger bridges, and energy-based models. The course will also examine emerging theoretical perspectives on foundation models and large-scale generative systems, including representation learning, self-supervised learning, and scaling laws. The course is intended for PhD students and advanced master's students interested in the mathematical and algorithmic foundations of modern deep learning and generative AI.

27-519.name: Simulation of Materials Processing
27-519.desc: This course deals with simulating materials at the length scale of their microstructure and macrostructure. These continuum-scale simulation methods are important tools for Materials Engineers. We will cover advanced classical thermodynamics and its implementation in the CALPHAD method, phase transformations in multicomponent systems and phase field models, and finite element modeling of mechanical behavior, heat flow, and fluid flow. The course will utilize available software, so the focus will be on materials fundamentals, not their computational implementation. Use cases for the various methods will be taken from materials processing operations. At the end of this class students should be able to describe the simulation methods, perform basic simulations, and critically interpret results.

21-317.name: Topics in Analysis
21-317.desc: This course affords students the opportunity to study topics in the area of expertise of the instructor. The course content will vary from semester to semester and may include advanced subjects within real analysis, functional analysis, complex analysis, or differential equations.  For example, topics may include: - Fixed point theory and applications to differential equations - Measure theory and integration - Functional analysis and operator theory - Topics in Fourier and harmonic analysis  Students may take this course more than once if the content differs substantially.

21-425.name: Probability and Martingales
21-425.desc: Probability is a fundamental tool that has found applications in most modern scientific fields. This course serves as an honors introduction to the subject. It will introduce the fundamentals (probability spaces, random variables, distributions) and then study independence, conditioning, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. Advanced topics covered after this may vary and may include martingales, stopping times, optional sampling, and optimal stopping problems. No previous familiarity with probability is required, however, the course is mathematically rigorous and some experience with reading and writing proofs is expected.

24-603.name: "Special Topics: TechSpark: Machine Shop Practice
24-603.desc: This course is intended for graduate-level students with prior shop experience.  Students in this course will practice the safe operation of manual machining equipment, including knee mill and lathe through structured hands-on activities. A significant portion of this course is dedicated to reading technical drawings, and then fabricating those components using equipment. Homework assignments are important for reinforcement of skills learned. This course is required to use the student machine shop at TechSpark. 3-unit mini (7-weeks)

24-889.name: Generative AI for Engineers
24-889.desc: This course equips engineers with the knowledge and tools to build, adapt, and apply generative AI models to solve complex engineering problems. This course focuses on foundational models and generative architectures—moving beyond usage and toward creation and customization of AI models tailored to engineering domains. Students will learn to implement and adapt key generative model families, including transformers, diffusion models, and neural operators, with an emphasis on engineering applications

57-288.name: Divas in Pop: from Madonna to Lady Gaga
57-288.desc: Pop divas have been revered in U.S. culture for their musical contributions, fashion, and entrepreneurship. This course will survey pop divas in the U.S. from Aretha Franklin to our current reigning divas like Taylor Swift and Chappel Roan, especially considering foundational divas Madonna and Cher to modern but seasoned divas like Beyonce and Lady Gaga. This course will contain individual and group work, presentations, a short paper, and projects for creative knowledge demonstration. Course work will include academic readings, public facing and pop culture readings, listening examples, podcast episodes, documentary/video screenings, and a trip to a local art museum.

80-328.name: Voting Theory
80-328.desc: Why bother voting?   When does a social problem admit a good solution through a feasible voting mechanism, and when not? This undergraduate course discusses fundamental concepts in voting theory.   We study formal and informal properties of rival voting schemes, including issues of constitutional design, voting paradoxes, and spatial models of candidates' and voters' strategic behaviors. We apply social choice theory to frame formal results: examining the Median Voter Theorem and Roberts Rules of Order as methods for choosing a Condorcet winner. We use historical examples to illustrate and inform our investigation: reviewing the evolution of the US electoral system for deciding Presidential elections. We contrast rival voting mechanisms through their varieties of tradeoffs among the qualitative and quantitative features that we associate with voting.

80-490.name: Philosophical and Practical Aspects of AI
80-490.desc: Artificial Intelligence has deep roots in both philosophy and computer science and has undergone major paradigm shifts, from symbolic AI to statistical learning, deep learning, foundation models, causal AI, and embodied AI. This course examines the historical development of AI, analyzing the motivations, strengths, and limitations of each paradigm, as well as the types of problems they aim to address. We explore foundational contributions from thinkers and scientists such as Aristotle, Augustine, Francis Bacon, Galileo Galilei, Isaac Newton, Immanuel Kant, Gottlob Frege, Alan Turing, Marvin Minsky, Herbert Simon, Judea Pearl, Geoffrey Hinton, Demis Hassabis, and Richard Sutton, among others. Through these perspectives, we investigate the philosophical foundations, practical advances, and societal implications of AI.

80-790.name: Philosophical and Practical Aspects of AI
80-790.desc: Artificial Intelligence has deep roots in both philosophy and computer science and has undergone major paradigm shifts, from symbolic AI to statistical learning, deep learning, foundation models, causal AI, and embodied AI. This course examines the historical development of AI, analyzing the motivations, strengths, and limitations of each paradigm, as well as the types of problems they aim to address. We explore foundational contributions from thinkers and scientists such as Aristotle, Augustine, Francis Bacon, Galileo Galilei, Isaac Newton, Immanuel Kant, Gottlob Frege, Alan Turing, Marvin Minsky, Herbert Simon, Judea Pearl, Geoffrey Hinton, Demis Hassabis, and Richard Sutton, among others. Through these perspectives, we investigate the philosophical foundations, practical advances, and societal implications of AI

69-132.name: Team Sports
69-132.desc: This course is designed to teach students the skills and foundation in the following three sports:  volleyball, soccer and basketball.    The course will spend 6-7 classes on each of these sports and rotate to a new one once the skills are developed and students understand the game and can successfully play the game.

33-431.name: Stars and Black Holes
33-431.desc: Stellar Astrophysics explores the physical principles governing stars, from their formation to their evolution on the main sequence and beyond, ultimately producing dense stellar remnants. This course will systematically describe the physics of stellar structure, radiation transport, nuclear fusion, and energy generation in order to provide a comprehensive survey of how stars evolve. Students will specifically study stellar evolution, supernovae, compact objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes, as well as binary interactions and gravitational waves. Where applicable, the course will incorporate the use of public software and data. This course requires both 33-331 and 33-341 as corequisites.

33-731.name: Stars and Black Holes
33-731.desc: Stellar Astrophysics explores the physical principles governing stars, from their formation to their evolution on the main sequence and beyond, ultimately producing dense stellar remnants. This course will systematically describe the physics of stellar structure, radiation transport, nuclear fusion, and energy generation in order to provide a comprehensive survey of how stars evolve. Students will specifically study stellar evolution, supernovae, compact objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes, as well as binary interactions and gravitational waves. Where applicable, the course will incorporate the use of public software and data. Students will develop analytical, numerical, and computational problem-solving skills essential for graduate research in stellar astrophysics and related fields.

33-788.name: Special Topics: AI in Particle Physics and Astrophysics

85-411.name: Introduction to Music Cognition Research
85-411.desc: This course explores the roles of cognitive processes in the experience of music with a focus on carrying out a collaborative laboratory project in order to understand first-hand the challenges of the experimental study of music. In readings, lectures, discussions, and demonstrations we will become acquainted with the relevant psychological theories of perception, memory and learning, and review and critically analyze selected experimental findings on the psychology of music. We will examine the use of psychological principles (e.g. Gestalt laws of perception, limitations on working memory, categorical perception, chunking, schemas, modularity) to explain musical phenomena. The emphasis will be on applying an experimental approach to music perception and cognition, but we will also consider ongoing debates about larger issues (such as musics adaptive value to the human species, and the determinants of musical taste). Prerequisite: either Harmony 1 or Cognitive Psychology or introduction to psychology or an intro level statistics or by instructor permission.

85-453.name: Stigma and its Consequences
85-453.desc: This seminar will introduce students to theoretical and empirical psychological research on prejudice and social stigma. The topics covered will include examinations of why individuals stigmatize: exploring cognitive, evolutionary, self, and system justification explanations. The course will examine the consequences of stigmatization for low-status groups (e.g., stereotype threat, dis-identification, internalization, health outcomes). We will explore the role of stigma in intergroup interactions and variation in the experience of stigma. Specific course topics will include the meaning of stigma, why people stigmatize, the physiological, cognitive-affective and social behavioral processes linking stigma and health outcomes, and moderators of stigma.

85-470.name: Frontiers in Brain and Behavior
85-470.desc: In addition to the core lectures of 85-170 Foundations of Brain and Behaviour, advanced undergraduates may enroll in a companion seminar that extends each topic to the research frontier. Through weekly discussions of recently published research—introducing novel methods, overturning prevailing assumptions, or reframing classic debates—students sharpen the critical thinking skills needed to engage with the evolving frontiers of brain and behaviour.  This will not fulfill an undergraduate advanced psychology seminar.

85-490.name: Clincial Science and Practice
85-490.desc: In this course, students will be exposed to the science and practice of clinical psychology, with a particular emphasis on the synergistic relationship between clinical psychological research and clinical practice. We will focus on the four major activities that clinical psychologists engage in (research, assessment, diagnosis, and psychotherapy). Students will learn about the clinical characteristics of major psychological disorders and the empirically-validated treatments available for these conditions. We will make frequent use of research findings and the scientific method to evaluate and understand concepts in clinical psychology. Critical thinking will be emphasized as we explore the scientific strengths and limitations of various treatments for psychological disorders. This course is designed to be a smaller seminar course for juniors and seniors considering graduate school in clinical psychology. Instructor permission is required, please email Dr. Crista Crittenden at  ccritten@andrew.cmu.edu.

90-914.name: Foundations of Information Systems Research
90-914.desc: Organizations and markets use a wide variety of structures to coordinate the productive activities of their stakeholders. Dramatic changes in information technology and the nature of economic competition are forcing firms to develop new ways of organizing work. Similarly, new types of digital information goods, much lower search costs, and improved targeting are changing the nature of many markets. This course uses economic theory to investigate the roles of information and technology in the existing diversity of organizations and markets and in enabling the creation of new organizational forms. The class is designed for Ph.D students in Information Systems, Economics, Organizational Behavior, and related disciplines. For economists, this class offers the opportunity to apply economic tools to understand how information technology and information in general affect organizations and markets. For non-economists, this class offers an exposure to fundamental ideas in the economics of information, organizations, and markets. The main goal is to prepare Ph.D. students to produce publication-quality research using tools from information economics.
90-914.department: Public Policy & Mgt:Sch of Pub Pol & Mgt

16-706.name: Robotic Foundations: Algebra
16-706.desc: Linear algebra underlies nearly every area of robotics, including perception, control, planning, estimation, and learning. In fact, many failures in modern robotic systems arise not from missing algorithms, but from misunderstandings of representation, geometry, conditioning, and observability.  This PhD-level mini course rebuilds a geometric and inferential understanding of linear algebra as it appears implicitly inside modern robotic systems. Rather than emphasizing formula memorization or procedural computation, the course treats linear algebra as a diagnostic language for reasoning about what a system can represent, what information is preserved or lost, when ambiguity is structural rather than statistical, and why certain failures occur silently rather than catastrophically.  The course follows a deliberate arc: (1) Representation and Geometry, (2) Inference and Stability, and (3) Degeneracy and Observability. Students revisit vectors, linear transformations, rank, least squares, eigenvalues, singular values, conditioning and projective geometry through formal definitions, geometric intuition, and modern robotics framing. This course is not a first introduction to linear algebra and is not programming-heavy. It is a compact, concept-driven reset intended to strengthen research-level reasoning in robotics.

16-707.name: Robotic Foundations: Optimization
16-707.desc: Numerical optimization is the foundation of contemporary robotics.  Optimization serves as the decision-making process that makes autonomy possible for complex robots acting in constrained environments with imperfect representations of the world surrounding them.  This course focuses heavily on the optimization methods that underpin model-based robotics, striking a balance between theory and practical implementation on “real” robotic systems.  Throughout the course, you will learn how to formulate and solve robotics problems such as numerical inverse kinematics, trajectory optimization, model predictive control, and optimal estimation using modern optimization tools. By the end of the course, you will be able to peer into the black box of contemporary optimization routines to understand their inner workings and to augment as necessary for your own research.

16-709.name: Robotic Foundations: Software Engineering
16-709.desc: This mini-course provides students with the foundational software skills required for getting started in robotics research. The curriculum covers topics ranging from local Linux setup and version control, to building basic integrated systems in ROS2. Students will spend the second half of the course specializing in the software implementation of basic applications in one of three streams - Navigation, Manipulation, or Robot Learning - by developing a project within specialized physics engines and toolsets.

07-380.name: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning II
07-380.desc: 07-380 is the second in a two-course sequence covering the breadth and depth of AI/ML required by the AI major/minor. Building upon 07-280 AI & ML I, 07-380 is designed to both solidify the fundamental components of AI and ML as well as introduce students to the latest breakthroughs in the rapidly changing AI landscape.

88-342.name: The Neuroscience of Decision Making
88-342.desc: Because we are human, feelings provide the basis for reason and rational decision-making. Consider for example, that brain-damaged patients left devoid of emotion struggle to make the most elementary decisions: while they are able layout the pros and cons of a decision, but they are unable to make the final choice. This course will discuss seminal discoveries in affective neuroscience underlying decision-making.

17-222.name: Introduction to Societal Computing
17-222.desc: This course provides an overview of the field of societal computing, its history, goals, methods, and applications. It introduces the key concepts and frameworks for analyzing the social and ethical implications of computing technology, such as privacy, security, fairness, accountability, and human values. The course will be centered around short, interactive lectures, accompanied with class discussions. Panels of invited Societal Computing faculty will be invited to synthesize and further explore the topics introduced in lectures. Students will also participate in active learning experiences involving the critical analysis of media and technology artifacts and take turns presenting and leading class discussions throughout the semester.

17-350.name: Safe Systems Programming in Rust
17-350.desc: Rust is transforming systems programming, giving developers the tools to write memory- and time-efficient code at a systems level of abstraction while providing safety guarantees stronger than most high-level languages.  This course will provide comprehensive coverage of safe systems programming techniques, using Rust as the vehicle of instruction although the techniques covered can be applied in other languages (typically with fewer static guarantees).  We will cover ownership types, safe manual memory management, safe concurrency, asynchronous code, and how to provide a safe interface that encapsulates unsafe code.  Students will practice these techniques while writing systems programs from a variety of domains, including threaded interpreters, webassembly executables in the browser, embedded device controllers, and distributed consistency protocols.  We will also cover Rust specifics, including ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, Rust's concurrency model, async, error handling, unsafe, the foreign function interface, traits, functional programming, reference counted pointers, modules and crates, and macros.

17-593.name: Hands-On Negotiations for Technology Leaders
17-593.desc: Negotiation skills are fundamental to professionals in all fields. Indeed, a strong argument can be made that almost every interaction that humans engage in is a negotiation in one form or another. This can be particularly important in technology-related industries and positions, where individuals may find themselves negotiating a job offer, attempting to convince upper management to back a new product or project, or trying to agree on deal terms for a corporate merger or a venture capital investment. The ability to identify your goals and alternatives, to effectively engage with a negotiating partner, and to define and achieve a positive outcome is critical to success in these and numerous other endeavors - and those who excel at handling these kinds of complex and often nuanced interactions will achieve greater success for themselves and their organizations.

17-650.name: Safe Systems Programming in Rust
17-650.desc: Rust is transforming systems programming, giving developers the tools to write memory- and time-efficient code at a systems level of abstraction while providing safety guarantees stronger than most high-level languages.  This course will provide comprehensive coverage of safe systems programming techniques, using Rust as the vehicle of instruction although the techniques covered can be applied in other languages (typically with fewer static guarantees).  We will cover ownership types, safe manual memory management, safe concurrency, asynchronous code, and how to provide a safe interface that encapsulates unsafe code.  Students will practice these techniques while writing systems programs from a variety of domains, including threaded interpreters, webassembly executables in the browser, embedded device controllers, and distributed consistency protocols.  We will also cover Rust specifics, including ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, Rust's concurrency model, async, error handling, unsafe, the foreign function interface, traits, functional programming, reference counted pointers, modules and crates, and macros.

17-732.name: Introduction to Accessibility and Assistive Technology
17-732.desc: This course will explore ability, disability, and accessibility. It introduces students to the theory, history, policy, and practice of accessibility and inclusion in computing. Course readings will explore relevant concepts from disability studies, accessibility, human-computer interaction, and design methods. Most accessibility content focuses on web accessibility for people who are blind or low-vision. In addition, through this course, you will learn how to design for people with different abilities including hearing loss, motor impairments, cognitive decline, and neurodiversity. As early adopters, people with disabilities have inspired a host of future user interface technologies, e.g., conversational assistants, text-to-speech, speech recognition, optical character recognition, predictive typing, tactile displays, etc. People with disabilities continue to be the first users of interface next-generation technologies that are gradually adopted widely. We will discuss how to design online and offline; how to design for visible and invisible disabilities; and how to design for permanent, situational, and temporary disabilities. This is a practice-oriented course, and students will work in multidisciplinary teams to brainstorm, develop, and evaluate some kind of tool or system with people with disabilities.

17-815.name: Writing Workshop for Computer Science Researchers
17-815.desc: A small-group course for PhD students who want to learn to write better research papers. Students will work on improving one of their own pieces of writing  --- ideally a research paper under preparation, but job materials or similar may also work.  Contact the instructor if you have questions. Weekly meetings will consist of short, practical exercises on research writing, along with regular writer's workshop sessions where the group reads and discusses each other's drafts in a structured, supportive format.  By the end of the course, students will have polished papers at or near submission quality; practical techniques for structuring, drafting, and revising research writing in general; and experience reading research writing critically and giving constructive feedback.  This course is designed to integrate with your existing graduate student research obligations. The bulk of the work will be on a paper you need to write anyway. Weekly preparation will be kept tractable, generally centered around reading parts of your peers' work.  Open to PhD students in SCS and ECE (or related areas) with a current research writing project.

36-319.name: Statistics and Machine Learning for the Physical Sciences
36-319.desc: In this course, we will learn about new methodological research at the intersection of statistics, machine learning, and AI with applications in the physical sciences (including meteorology, remote sensing, astronomy, and particle physics). Students will see examples of how core statistical ideas (confidence sets, hypothesis testing, two-sample testing, and uncertainty quantification) play a key role in cutting-edge research in predictive inference, probabilistic forecasting, anomaly or signal detection, and likelihood-free (aka simulator-based) inference. Homework assignments will include assigned reading, theory problems, and some simple computer exercises. Students will work with real-world data during TA-led computer labs using Python/PyTorch and Jupyter notebooks to apply the skills and knowledge acquired throughout the program. (Prior exposure to Python programming is not required.) The course assumes a solid foundation in the theory of probability and statistical inference at the level of 36-226, but this pre-requisite can be waived at the discretion of the instructor (e.g., for students in Mellon College of Science).

36-631.name: Foundations of Causal Inference
36-631.desc: This course will provide an introduction to the fundamentals of causal inference. Causal inference is concerned with whether and how one can go beyond statistical associations to draw causal conclusions from observational data. Topics will include: counterfactuals (potential outcomes and graphs), identification and estimation of average treatment effects in experiments and observational studies, nonparametric bounds, sensitivity analysis, instrumental variables, effect modification, and longitudinal studies.

36-632.name: Modern Causal Inference
36-632.desc: This course will provide an in-depth look at modern causal inference. Topics will include: optimal treatment regimes, mediation, principal stratification, stochastic interventions, accounting for complex confounding and exposures, and methods for efficient nonparametric estimation. Some background in mathematical statistics is advised.

36-740.name: Advanced Methods I- Data over Space and Time
36-740.desc: A survey of methods for spatial, temporal and spatio-temporal statistics, with an emphasis on tools which can be applied in all three domains: Optimal linear prediction / estimation / de-noising ("Wiener filter", "kriging"); covariance function estimation, including low-rank approximations ("factor models"); state-space modeling and state estimation ("Kalman filter", "particle filter"); generative models and point processes; resampling methods for bootstrapping.

36-741.name: Advanced Methods II- Simulation-Based Inference
36-741.desc: An introduction to methods for doing statistical inference for generative models where calculating the likelihood is intractable, but running simulations is easy.  Classic methods of point estimation ("method of simulated generalized monents"; "indirect inference"; "approximate Bayesian computation"); uncertainty quantification and hypothesis testing; neural-network techniques; random-feature methods.

98-396.name: The Mandarin Gateway: Communication and Culture Decoded

98-398.name: Principles of Baking
98-398.desc: Principles of Baking: Explore the chemistry and technique behind bread, pastries, cakes, and more, to learn how recipes work. Walk away with the practical skills to bake with confidence. No prior experience needed.

98-399.name: Fundamentals of Trading and Technical Analysis with Cryptocurrencies

98-401.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): The Hidden Worlds of Studio Ghibli
98-401.desc: From the post-war tragedy of “Grave of the Fireflies” to the fantastical romance of “Howl’s Moving Castle,” Studio Ghibli’s films have captivated audiences all over the world with their heartfelt messages and perilous journeys. This course invites students to examine and explore the films throughout the course of the semester. Students will be expected to participate in in-class activities, complete assignments in a timely manner (including take-home quizzes), take a midterm, and complete a final project of their choice. There is no prerequisite; whether you have watched all of the films or none, you are welcome! Ideally, students will end the semester with a deeper understanding and appreciation of the worlds within the Ghibli films, and the world outside that shaped their creation.

98-402.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Evolution of Video Games
98-402.desc: Video games are an inherently weird form of entertainment. They combine drawing, animation, music, and almost every other possible form of entertainment. Because of this, video games have evolved dramatically throughout the evolution of technology in the past thirty years. Since video games are designed to engage humans, the way humans interact with games is unique.   Since the widespread adoption of the internet in our day-to-day lives, the way we consume video games has changed from being merely a fun toy at an arcade to a career where people make a good living.   In this course, we will delve into how video games have gone from being a mere novelty to the most profitable form of entertainment by a significant margin. The core idea of this course is learning how human interaction has inherently altered the way video games are produced and made. Knowing how video games have evolved will help students understand how products evolve to adapt to the wants of the consumer, and how consumption of a product can contribute to its creation. Additionally, through this course, students will gain a brief overview of how our own minds work, habits, and how understanding these things can influence our own behavior.  Some familiarity with video games is recommended, but this class can be taken without any knowledge of video games.

98-403.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Anime: Power, Plot, and Personas
98-403.desc: Lecture slides will go over the history of famous authors, psychological research, and narrative storytelling. During the course, students will learn different storytelling elements (e.g., personality, character design, motivation, etc) and create their own characters/stories. Lecture, presentation, and Discussion-Based No prior knowledge necessary, enlighten us with your anime facts!

98-404.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo) Pokemon GO Gaming in Public Spaces
98-404.desc: Welcome to Pokémon GO: Gaming in Public Spaces! Even ten years after the 2016 craze, Pokémon GO remains one of the most-played mobile games, with an active community in Oakland and Squirrel Hill. This course will teach you the fundamentals of how to play, connect you with other players, and give you tools to engage more deeply with the game. If you don’t have an account, you’ll learn how to create one and navigate the interface, which can be confusing for new players. You’ll catch your first Pokémon, strengthen your team, and learn both main battle systems: Gyms and Trainer Battles. Later in the course, we’ll explore higher-level topics to help you improve your gameplay, understand AR’s role in daily life, and evaluate Pokémon through appraisal and optimization strategies. You’ll also learn where to find more players in Pittsburgh and beyond.  Classes will be taught mostly through weekly lectures with live demonstrations and examples to explain core mechanics. Grades will be based on participation, short writing assignments to reflect on your progress, and in-game milestones that match course content.  Pokémon GO is more than a game—it uses augmented reality to change how you interact with your environment. You’ll come to understand Pittsburgh’s geography in new ways, meet people outside CMU, and explore how statistical and computational systems shape gameplay. The course highlights the intersection of nature, technology, and culture, helping you see why Pokémon GO continues to influence cities, transportation, and community-building.  All students are welcome. Those familiar with Pokémon may know some of the early material, but the course is designed to ensure that everyone has an equally positive and engaging experience.

98-405.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Introduction to Arknights
98-405.desc: Arknights is an anime-style 2D tower defense RPG that has gained worldwide popularity since its release in 2019. Its creation has almost single-handedly taken its creator Hypergryph from a small, unknown company to the big name in mobile gacha gaming it is today. In this course, we approach Arknights from two lenses: a tower defense game perspective, using it to improve students’ strategic thinking; as well as a game design perspective, analyzing features and background story to see why it is as well-received as it is. Students will explore concepts about the game, different use cases for different characters, how to combine tactics to beat difficult levels and succeed in unknown ones, and, of course, experience the wonder of game design that is Arknights.

98-406.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Learn To Knit
98-406.desc: This beginner-friendly knitting course will teach you fundamental techniques to design and create your own garment. The course covers materials, knitting terminology, gauge swatching, and scaling your swatches. The basic skills and techniques taught in the course are designed to prepare you for your midterm and final projects. The midterm will require you to develop a design plan for a garment of your choice. The final project will be the execution of that plan. Through class sessions and homework assignments, you will gain familiarity with knitting. Class sessions will take the form of informational sessions on knitting techniques, demonstrations, and time for students to complete independent work. Yes, some days you will come to class to simply knit in a group!

98-407.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Storytime: I Survived the Internet Drama
98-407.desc: The world has become more virtual, and we are constantly surrounded by online news. In this course, students will learn about various moments of Internet drama, primarily controversies around popular online figures, such as Shane Dawson, Miranda Sings, and Mr. Beast. Students will also learn how to engage in online discourse, develop their own opinions, and assess opposing viewpoints. To achieve this, students will provide a creative case study and participate in a Model UN-style debate to defend their perspective.

98-408.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Philosophy in Pop Culture
98-408.desc: Philosophy is often seen as a purely academic subject, precluding many from participating in it. But what if it didn't have to be like that? This course will examine traditional philosophical ideas, but through the lens of pop culture institutions we usually interact with casually. How should we theorize about the future... while watching Black Mirror? What constitutes a useful ethical framework... as seen in Futurama? How sure should we be of our religious beliefs... as examined through The Good Place? You will leave this course more knowledgeable about philosophy, but critically, more aware of the philosophical implications in the world around you, even in the places you'd never expect it.

98-409.name: Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Introduction to Rhythm Games
98-409.desc: This course will serve as a both comprehensive and flexible introduction to rhythm games. Throughout the course, you will be exposed to more and more different rhythm games. As you play more and more, you could build your own skills in a wide variety of games, while learning to analyze and appreciate charts (“levels”) and the structure and artistry behind them. After we cover the basics of charting and the usage of charting tools, you will craft your own chart for the game you love the most!  While class time will only be an hour a week, homework is emphasized as the most important learning time for students, as it allows you to both hone their skills and allow for exploration/exposure to more charts. By the end of the course, you will have the general skills to play a variety of games, understand charts on a deeper level, and be able to create original charts.  This course has no prerequisites, just be interested and have fun!

76-768.name: Public Speaking
76-768.desc: This course, designed for students who want to boost their confidence in presenting in front of others, is an introduction to the study and practice of public speaking: the skill of conveying your thoughts and ideas in a compelling manner for your intended audience. This involves, first and foremost, practice: we will focus on improving your ability to speak confidently, eloquently, and engagingly in front of an audience through regular practice of presentation and delivery. However, this course also takes the perspective that being an eloquent speaker requires being a strong critical and rhetorical thinker, as well as a perceptive reader of persuasive texts of all kinds. To that end, you will engage in some theoretical dimensions of speech and persuasion through required readings, class discussions, rhetorical and speech analyses, and written assignments, learning strategies to approach, research, and organize instances of public speech to convey your ideas memorably and effectively.  Attendance on speech days is mandatory. Grades will be based on improvement and effort in order to encourage students to focus on their development rather than on final outcomes.  This course is designed to strengthen skills that are crucial to your development as an informed and engaged citizen and future professional, as well those skills that will prove immediately useful to you as a university student.

70-445.name: Artificial Intelligence for Business Leaders
70-445.desc: This course examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizations, industries, and managerial decision-making. Designed as a flagship, practice-oriented course, it equips current and aspiring business leaders with the tools to evaluate, design, and communicate AI-driven initiatives across core business functions. Students engage with real-world business problems in marketing, finance, operations, supply chain management, and people analytics to assess where AI creates value and where it does not. Across the semester, students learn to balance technical capabilities with organizational readiness, governance, ethics, and regulation. Topics such as privacy, bias, transparency, workforce transformation, and risk management are integrated throughout, emphasizing responsible and sustainable adoption of intelligent technologies.

57-265.name: Introduction to Composition
57-265.desc: Exploration of various methods of music composition and study of fundamental compositional devices through a series of listening assignments and composition projects in both traditional and contemporary styles. Students will also learn and develop artistic sensitivity through non-musical elements including silence, emotion, text, and image.
