57-579.name: Assessment in Music and Learning
57-579.desc: This course includes a study in current and historical assessment practice and theory in music education. The course will culminate in the creation of a unit of study with assessments for a music education course of the student's choice

57-765.name: Introduction to Composition
57-765.desc: Exploration of various methods of music composition and study of fundamental compositional devices through a series of listening assignments and composition projects in both traditional and contemporary styles. Students will also learn and develop artistic sensitivity through non-musical elements including silence, emotion, text, and image.

85-210.name: Language and Thought
85-210.desc: The basic goal of the course is to understand the nature of language and how it relies on cognitive mechanics to express thought.  This question can be unpacked into a series of more specific questions.  What is unique about human language?  What is unique about human thought? What are the genetic, physiological, and social bases for language? How did language evolve?  How does the brain process language? What causes language impairments? How do children learn language? How do people learn second languages? Are there language universals? How and why do languages change over time? What are the relations between language and thought? What are the relations between language and gesture? What are the practical consequences of understanding these issues? How can machines be taught to use language? What can we learn from machines that process language? There are two major approaches to these issues: the established theory of Universal Grammar and the newer theory of Emergentism.  We will review both, but we will elaborate the newer approach in more detail.

18-395.name: Introduction to Computer Vision
18-395.desc: The course introduces students to basics of computer vision to build familiarity with basic vision concepts, problems, and tools. The course covers the early image formation pipeline (how an image is formed on a sensor and how a camera processes it), basic image processing techniques, 3D perception from single, double and multiple views, semantic scene understanding, optical flow and motion modeling, and the use of learning-based approaches for solving these problems. Course will have biweekly homework, weekly quizzes, a midterm and a final exam.

85-103.name: Possible Minds: Exploring Intelligence in Science Fiction
85-103.desc: This course uses readings ranging from classic to contemporary science fiction to examine fundamental questions about the nature of intelligence across human, artificial, and possible alien minds. Through short stories and novel excerpts, we will explore themes such as consciousness, identity, memory, perception, free will, and the boundaries of personhood and social intelligence, connecting imaginative and prescient narratives to current scientific, philosophical, and societal debates. Class discussions will use fiction as a lens for investigating what it means to be intelligent.

17-739.name: Special Topics in Cybersecurity: Machine Learning for Cybersecurity
17-739.desc: Cybersecurity has become a high-stakes battlefield, and machine learning is both a weapon and a shield. From home IoT devices to critical infrastructure, the stakes have never been higher: the attack surface of our systems keeps increasing; attackers are more and more determined and sophisticated; and ML is emerging as a tool to automate attacks. This course will explore the most significant uses of ML for cybersecurity over the past four decades while focusing on the most promising defenses proposed in recent years. Example applications that will be covered are malware detection, spam detection, anomaly detection for computer networks, anomaly detection for industrial control systems, generating private synthetic data, vulnerability detection, and assisting in security-relevant decision-making by both security experts and end users. The course will also teach students to think critically about the challenges and pitfalls of applying ML to cybersecurity, such as the base rate fallacy, unavailability of training data, lack of interpretability of ML models, and susceptibility of ML models to adversarial examples.

04-646.name: Cloud Computing Systems
04-646.desc: Previously called Cloud Infrastructure and Computing, this course introduces the fundamentals of cloud computing, including core services like compute, storage, networking, and databases. It covers key models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and deployment types (public, private, hybrid). Students gain hands-on experience with AWS, Azure, and GCP, learning to deploy, manage, scale, and secure cloud applications, along with topics such as virtualization, containers, serverless computing, and cloud storage.

04-722.name: Cybersecurity Operations
04-722.desc: This course is designed to provide students with practical experience in cybersecurity incident detection and response in a real-world setting. In this course, students will get an in-depth understanding of Security Operations Center (SOC) roles and responsibilities, as well as the open-source technologies used to detect, analyze, track and respond to security incidents. Students will gain practical skills in SOC operations, including continuous monitoring, threat intelligence, threat hunting, incident response, use of SOC tools, as well as managing and tuning them. The course combines theoretical knowledge with hands-on labs to prepare students for real world security challenges to get them started as TIER I SOC analysts.

04-733.name: AIOps: Continuous and Automated IT and AI Monitoring
04-733.desc: This course builds on and integrates S/W engineering, AI/ML, and IT skills in support of automated methods for assuring the highest level of system availability and resilience.  Students will apply tools including Docker and AI-based models for anomaly detection to monitor and correct hybrid cloud applications as they experience simulated disruptions and outages.  Lab exercises will deploy such monitoring tools in continuous integration/delivery pipelines for pro-active control as opposed to traditional reactive and manual incident response. The course will focus on automated monitoring of both IT components (e.g. code-based implementations of a distributed application) and AI/ML components (e.g. models and their associated pre- and post- deployment pipelines).    The course requires prior background in DevOps including Docker, CI/CD pipelines, and the microservices architectures used in hybrid cloud deployments.  This background provides preparation for deep dives on real-time operational data gathering and the automated tools available for anomaly detection, reporting, and even self-correction.      For IT monitoring, multiple types of performance data will be used in automated monitoring including structured metrics such as CPU, memory, and network utilization as well as emerging methods using large language models for analyzing unstructured content such as textual information in application logs.    For AI monitoring, extensions of DevIOps methods for AI will introduce ModelOps and its application to multiple types of quality metrics for automated model monitoring.  Model accuracy, precision, recall, and bias will be evaluated for initial deployment and tracked for post-deployment drift over time leading to predicted violation of quality standards.

04-751.name: Reinforcement Learning
04-751.desc: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamentals and advanced topics of Reinforcement Learning (RL), focusing on how autonomous agents can learn to make optimal decisions through interaction with an environment. Unlike supervised learning, RL focuses on learning from sparse, delayed rewards—a critical component for building intelligent engineering systems such as autonomous robots, smart grids, and adaptive manufacturing pipelines.  The course bridges classical RL theory with modern Deep Learning techniques. Students will explore how to represent complex state spaces using neural networks and how to stabilize learning in high-dimensional environments. A significant portion of the course is dedicated to the "Sim-to-Real" challenge, preparing students to deploy AI models in physical world scenarios relevant to the African context and global engineering standards.

04-782.name: Energy Data Analytics
04-782.desc: The energy transition in Africa presents significant challenges but also opportunities for sustainable development on the continent. Data is poised to play an important role in ensuring that this transition is realized in an equitable, efficient, and timely manner. This course equips graduate students with the analytical frameworks and practical Python-based tools to extract actionable insight from energy data in African contexts. The course is designed for two complementary audiences: energy professionals and engineers seeking to build rigorous data analytics capabilities, and data scientists and IT professionals seeking grounding in energy systems, policy, and sector-specific data challenges. Students from both tracks will work on shared applied projects, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of real-world energy analytics work. Topics span the full analytics pipeline — from data acquisition, cleaning, and exploratory analysis through to time series modeling, geospatial analysis, machine learning applications, and data-driven policy communication. All analytical work is grounded in African energy datasets, institutions, and policy frameworks, with case studies drawn from across Africa.

82-713.name: Support Strategies for Professional Translation
82-713.desc: This course supports the development of interpretive and translational competence.  Through whole-class workshops and individualized consultations, students in this course will strengthen their ability to analyze nuance, implied intention, rhetorical positioning, register, and voice across diverse text types.  This analysis will be furthered through practice reproducing those elements for specific or general target audiences across specified genres. Using texts drawn from their concurrent coursework—such as journalistic reporting, opinion/editorial writing, public-facing communications, and others—students will interpret implicit meaning, identify voice and stance, as well as manage tone and register. Emphasis is placed on transferable strategies that can be applied across evolving academic and professional situations.

80-684.name: Linguistics of Turkic Language
80-684.desc: In this course we look at languages from within a single language group, Turkic. Turkic languages are spoken across continental Asia and include such languages as Turkmen, Tatar, Kazakh, Uighur, and Uzbek. In this course we concentrate especially on Yakut (Sakha) and Azerbaijani. Modern Turkish will provide a reference language. We look at various linguistic systems within each language (phonology, morphology, syntax, and writing systems) both to understand each particular language and to see how the languages are related. We consider the impact of diachronic factors on the synchronic study of language. This course can be seen as an extended case-study for applying concepts and analytical strategies from basic linguistics, as taught in Nature of Language, Phonetics and Phonology, Invented Languages, and other relevant courses.

48-646.name: Urban Moss: Interstitial Space as Micro-Infrastructure
48-646.desc: This course investigates the potentials of micro-infrastructures built within the interstices of urban landscapes. Like moss—a plant known for its reciprocal benefits that create conditions for other species to thrive—this seminar explores how bottom-up interventions can foster a more vibrant public realm. Amid large-scale planning efforts, interstitial spaces often remain underutilized as a civic resource. This course positions these spaces as critical sites for experimentation and engagement with local communities.   Beginning with the emergence of public space theory in the 1960s, students will examine how these ubiquitous residual spaces have been transformed and activated over time.Through the decoding of contemporary case studies and on-site fieldwork, students will develop spatial propositions that operate reciprocally within the built environment, transforming underutilized spaces into a distributed network of socially and ecologically responsive interventions.

84-614.name: Politics, Technological Change, and Economic Growth
84-614.desc: Technological change has had an extraordinary impact on the story of humankind.   It has had a massive influence on the nature of our political systems.  It has been one of, maybe the, major determinant of economic growth and the way that wealth is distributed.   This class looks at this in the far past (100,000 BCE to 1600 ACE), the past (the Enlightenment and the subsequent industrial revolutions), the present day, and the future.  We will contemplate the future impact of AI on jobs, the nature of government, living standards, and equity.
84-614.department: CM Institute for Strategy and Tech

57-854.name: Advanced Acting for Singers
57-854.desc: In this upper-level course, we will dive deeper into the study and implementation of Stanislavsky's System and Active Analysis. Over the course of the semester, students will apply this technique to various scenes, monologues, and arias. This course is a shared creative space for artists to explore work that is compelling and meaningful to them. At times, students will be required to bring their own material to the table. They can support work that is being explored in other courses, lessons, or productions.

99-023.name: CMUPD Citizens Police Academy
99-023.desc: Discover what it’s like to be a part of law enforcement at Carnegie Mellon University! The Citizens Police Academy offers an inside look at the training, responsibilities, and community partnerships that define our department.  Join us for this engaging, hands-on experience. Don’t miss the opportunity to learn directly from CMUPD officers, ask questions, and gain valuable insights into campus safety and policing.  CMU's Citizens Police Academy is a six-week course for faculty and staff held on Wednesday evenings at 300 South Craig Street (building attached to the CMU Police Station).  The purpose of the Academy is to help bridge the gap between the CMU Police Department and the greater CMU community. Participants will learn more about the different training techniques, education and barriers that police officers face daily.  The CMU Police Department hopes this experience will help educate the CMU community about the role and functions of CMU police and foster deeper connections and understandings between the students, faculty, staff and officers to create more positive interactions and a safer community. The department also hopes to dispel myths and misconceptions about our department and all police.

70-379.name: Project Management
70-379.desc: This course equips students with the globally recognized frameworks, tools, and analytical techniques used to plan, execute, and deliver projects across business, technology, and operations contexts. Aligned with the PMI PMBOK Guide and Agile Practice Guide, the course covers the full project lifecycle alongside AI-enabled and data-driven decision-making. Students gain the foundational knowledge needed to pursue CAPM or PMP certification.
